examples.professional: In my commentary notes, I marked that Zechariah is identified as the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo.
examples.analytical: The genealogical identification of Zechariah as son of Berechiah shows the prophet's family was carefully recorded in postexilic tradition.

nuance.analogy: Like a name on a family tree, Berechiah connects one person to the generation before him.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew name meaning "Yahweh blesses," from the Hebrew roots for "bless" and the divine name.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with the stress on the first syllable, as in "BER-ih-kigh-uh."
Confusing the prophet Zechariah's father with his grandfather Iddo.
nuance.biblical_note: Berechiah, from the Hebrew Berekhyah, appears as a name of several men. Zechariah 1:1 identifies the prophet Zechariah as the son of Berechiah and the grandson of Iddo. 1 Chronicles 6:39 names Berechiah as the father of Asaph, a Levite musician. 2 Chronicles 28:12 mentions another Berechiah among the leaders of Ephraim.

senses.definition: To watch multiple episodes or issues of a certain content, such as television or Internet program, in a short period of time.

core.definition: To watch many episodes of a television show or series back-to-back in a short period, often using streaming services.

pronunciation.tip: Stress binge more strongly than watch, and keep watch short and crisp, with an 'ah' vowel like 'cot' in American speech. Do not stretch it into 'weatch'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a fun, relaxing habit, though some people see it as a waste of time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use binge-watch all the time in conversations about Netflix, Hulu, HBO and other streaming platforms. You might say you binge-watched a whole season over the weekend. A natural reply is 'Oh, I've been meaning to start that one!' In formal writing, the hyphen is standard.

distinctions.note: A marathon is a long session of watching TV, often a set of episodes in a row on a channel, while binge-watch specifically refers to streaming and watching episodes in quick succession.
Watch is a general verb, while binge-watch means watching many episodes quickly, often in one long session.

antonyms: watch one episode at a time

examples.everyday: I binge-watched the whole season last night, so I'm going to be tired at work today.
examples.professional: Several people on the team binge-watched the new training series, so the completion rates look really strong this quarter.
examples.analytical: Binge-watching changes how viewers experience narrative pacing, because the episodes blur together into one continuous story.

nuance.analogy: Binge-watching is like reading a whole book in one sitting instead of waiting for the next chapter each week.
nuance.etymology: Compound of binge and watch, popularized in the 2010s with streaming services.
common_mistakes: Writing 'binge watch' without the hyphen in formal writing, where the hyphenated form is standard.
Using binge-watch as a noun without the -ing form, as in 'a binge-watch' instead of 'binge-watching' or 'a binge-watching session'.

conversation.text: I binge-watched the whole show this weekend.
Let's binge-watch something tonight; I'm too tired to go out.
It's the perfect show to binge-watch on a rainy day.

senses.definition: Very crowded and slow-moving, particularly with regard to motor vehicle traffic.
(of a vehicle warranty) Comprehensive; covering all components.

core.definition: Describes traffic so dense that cars are packed closely together and moving slowly or stopped.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on the second 'bumper', and the first has secondary stress. The 'to' is reduced to 'tuh' in normal speech, and the r in both syllables is American r-colored.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes frustrating traffic or delays, though it can be neutral in a warranty context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use bumper-to-bumper for heavy traffic on freeways, especially during rush hour, as in 'the freeway was bumper-to-bumper'. In car shopping, bumper-to-bumper warranty is a common term for full coverage of most parts. The phrase is informal enough for everyday talk and common in news traffic reports.

distinctions.note: Gridlock means traffic is completely stopped across multiple intersections, while bumper-to-bumper describes dense, often slow-moving traffic that may still be moving.
Rush hour is the time period of heavy traffic, while bumper-to-bumper describes the traffic condition itself.

examples.everyday: Don't take the 405 today, it's bumper-to-bumper all the way to downtown.
examples.professional: Our traffic data shows the delivery routes are bumper-to-bumper between 4 and 6 p.m., so we should reschedule some stops.
examples.analytical: A bumper-to-bumper jam reveals how small individual choices can collectively produce a system that no driver intended.

nuance.analogy: Think of bumper-to-bumper traffic like sardines packed in a can, but on wheels, with no room to move.
nuance.etymology: From bumper, the bar on the front and back of a car, plus the phrase to bumper, describing cars touching nose to tail.
common_mistakes: Writing bumper to bumper without hyphens in formal writing, where the hyphenated adjective is standard.
Using it for a single slow car rather than a dense line of traffic.
Mispronouncing the middle 'to' as a full word with strong stress instead of 'tuh'.

conversation.text: Traffic was bumper-to-bumper all the way to the beach.
It's bumper-to-bumper on the bridge again, so I'll be late.
We spent the holiday weekend in bumper-to-bumper traffic.

senses.definition: In a manner which strictly adheres to rules, legal requirements, or official procedures.
In a manner which appears too studied, ritualized, and therefore artificial.

core.definition: Following rules, procedures, or official guidelines exactly, sometimes in a way that seems too strict.

pronunciation.tip: Say by with a long i, and the before a consonant is reduced to thuh. Book has the short oo sound of look, not the long oo of boot.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive when praising correct procedure and negative when it implies rigidity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use by the book in workplaces, sports, and everyday talk, as in she does everything by the book. It can compliment someone's careful work or criticize someone for being too rigid. A common reply is 'Yeah, she's a real stickler for the rules.'

distinctions.note: Both mean following rules, but by the book is more idiomatic and conversational.
Rigid is negative and describes inflexibility, while by the book can be praise for correct procedure.

examples.everyday: My landlord does everything by the book, so I always get my deposit back.
examples.professional: Let's follow the security review process by the book so the audit doesn't flag anything.
examples.analytical: Her interpretation is by the book, yet it leaves no room for the interpretive judgment the text demands.

nuance.analogy: Like following a recipe exactly with no changes.
nuance.etymology: Refers to a rulebook or official manual; the sense of strictly following written rules is well established in English.
common_mistakes: Using the plural by the books, which is not the standard idiom
Using it to praise something that is simply nice or good, when it means following rules strictly

conversation.text: Our new manager does everything by the book, even the expense reports.
Let's do this by the book so we don't have any issues with the audit.
He's a great cop because he goes by the book.

senses.definition: A casual goodbye (a little old-fashioned).

core.definition: A casual goodbye used when you expect to talk or see the person again soon.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NOW, and 'for' is weak, so it sounds like 'fer'. Pronounce bye with a clear long i sound, and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Warm and friendly. It suggests you will talk again, which makes it feel gentle rather than final.
nuance.usage_note: This phrase sounds a little old-fashioned, so you will hear it more from older speakers, in greeting cards or in friendly notes and voicemails. On the phone, people more often say 'Talk to you later' or 'Bye for now' to end a call with someone they know well. A natural reply is simply 'Bye, take care' or 'Bye for now.'

distinctions.note: Goodbye is neutral and used everywhere, while bye for now implies a short separation and a friendly feeling about the next contact.
Talk to you later is more common in modern casual speech and more specifically promises a phone call or chat.

collocations: bye for now and take care

examples.everyday: Okay, I have to run to the store. Bye for now, and tell the kids I said hi!
examples.professional: Thanks for the update on the pipeline. Bye for now, and I'll send the notes by Friday.
examples.analytical: Her closing 'bye for now' signaled that the conversation was paused rather than concluded.

nuance.analogy: Like a hand wave at a train platform: you expect to see the person again soon, so the parting is light.
nuance.etymology: Bye is a shortening of 'good-bye,' and 'for now' means for the present time.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing bye like 'bee' instead of the long i sound 'bye'.
Using it as a greeting at the start of a call instead of only at the end.

conversation.text: OK, I'll call you tomorrow. Bye for now.
That's all I needed. Thanks, and bye for now!
"Bye for now," she said, and hung up.

can-you-send-someone-to-take-a-look.phonetic: /kæn ju ˌsɛnd ˌsʌmˌwən tu ˌteɪk ə ˈlʊk/

senses.definition: Asking a landlord or company to send a repair person.

core.definition: A polite request asking a landlord, company or service desk to send a technician or repair person to check a problem.

pronunciation.ipa: /kæn ju sɛnd ˈsʌmwən tə teɪk ə ˈlʊk/
pronunciation.respelling: kan yoo send SUM-wun tuh tayk uh LOOK
pronunciation.tip: 'Someone' is stressed on the first syllable, SUM-, and the second syllable is reduced to 'wun'. 'To' reduces to /tə/ and 'a' to /ə/, so the phrase flows quickly. Stress LOOK, the final content word.

nuance.connotation: Polite and reasonable. It sounds cooperative and specific about what you need.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this when calling a landlord, property manager, or customer service about a broken appliance or leak. It is clear, polite, and works on the phone. A natural reply is 'Sure, I'll send someone out tomorrow morning' or 'We can have someone there by Friday.'

distinctions.note: 'Send someone out' is shorter and equally natural; 'take a look' adds the sense of inspecting the problem.
'Can you fix this?' asks for the repair directly, while this phrase asks for an inspection first, which is common when the problem is unclear.

collocations: send someone to take a look
can you send someone to take a look at the sink
send someone out to take a look
have someone come take a look

examples.everyday: Hi, the heater's making a loud noise. Can you send someone to take a look?
examples.professional: Hello, this is Priya in Unit 4B. Can you send someone to take a look at the leak under the sink this week?
examples.analytical: Requests for maintenance often reveal how responsibility is distributed, since asking someone to take a look assumes they have the authority to diagnose the problem.

nuance.analogy: It works like calling a doctor's office: you describe the symptom and ask for someone to examine it.
common_mistakes: Saying 'Can you send a person to take look?' and dropping 'a' before 'look'; the American phrase is 'take a look'.
Using 'send somebody' without 'to', as in 'send someone take a look'; 'to take' is needed.

conversation.text: The dishwasher is leaking. Can you send someone to take a look?
The heater's making a loud noise. Can you send someone to take a look today?
Can you send someone to take a look at the bathroom fan?

senses.definition: A member of the peoples who lived in the land of Canaan before the Israelites settled there.

core.definition: A member of the peoples who lived in the land of Canaan before the Israelites settled there.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, then the -ite ending is a long 'i' as in 'bite'. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, so it is kay-nuh-nite, not kay-NAY-ite.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive; in religious contexts it can carry negative implications because of its role in the conquest narratives.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Canaanite mainly in biblical and historical contexts. It can be a noun for a people or an adjective for their language, religion, or culture. Be careful, because the word can sound loaded in discussions about the conquest of the land.

distinctions.note: Hebrew is a language and a people in the Bible; Canaanite is a broader term for the pre-Israelite inhabitants of the land.
Amorite is another ancient people in the region, and the Bible often names them alongside Canaanites.

examples.everyday: My Sunday school teacher said the Canaanites lived in the hill country before the Israelites arrived.
examples.professional: The archaeology report compares pottery from several Canaanite sites in the region.
examples.analytical: The Old Testament treats the Canaanites as a people whose presence raises questions about divine judgment and covenant loyalty.

nuance.analogy: The Canaanites are like the first tenants of a house before a new family moves in: their presence shapes the house's history.
nuance.etymology: From Canaan plus the suffix -ite, 'belonging to'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in kuh-NAY-nite.
Using Canaanite to mean any ancient people of the Middle East.
nuance.biblical_note: Canaanites are the inhabitants of Canaan named throughout the Old Testament. Genesis 10:15-19 describes the descendants of Canaan and their territories. Exodus 3:8 lists the Canaanites among the peoples of the promised land. Joshua 3:10 names them in the account of Israel's entry into the land.

senses.definition: The position of champion, or winner.
Defense or support of some cause.
senses.example: His championship of civil rights eventually bore fruit.

senses.definition: A competition to determine a champion, especially the final of a series of competitions.

core.definition: A contest held to decide the best team or player, or the title won in that contest.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The -ion ending sounds like un, not ee-on, and the final -ship has a short i.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests achievement, competition, and excellence.
nuance.usage_note: In American sports, the championship usually means the final game or series that decides the top winner, such as the Super Bowl or the World Series. People often say win the championship or make it to the championship. A natural reply to Are you going to the championship? is Yeah, I'm really excited.

distinctions.note: A tournament is the whole competition with many rounds; the championship is usually the final event that decides the winner.
A title is the honor of being champion; championship can refer to the contest itself or to the status.
Playoffs are elimination rounds that lead to the final; the championship is usually the last of them.

examples.everyday: Are you watching the championship tonight, or are you too nervous to see the ending?
examples.professional: Our team is in the regional championship, so we're moving the sprint review to Friday.
examples.analytical: Winning a championship is often treated as proof of a team's excellence, yet a single final can reflect luck as much as skill.

nuance.analogy: Like a final exam at the end of a semester: it decides the top result for the whole course.
nuance.etymology: From champion plus the suffix -ship, meaning the state or position of being a champion.
common_mistakes: Using championship for the whole season; it usually refers to the final contest
Saying the championship of a sport in a stiff way; Americans say the state championship or win the championship

conversation.text: They won the championship three years in a row.
The championship game is on Sunday night.
Our high school team made it to the state championship.

senses.definition: To talk a while in a friendly manner.
senses.example: I met my old friend in the street, so we chatted for a while.

senses.definition: To talk of; to discuss.
senses.example: They chatted politics for a while.

senses.definition: To be engaged in informal conversation.
senses.example: She chatted with her friend in the cafe.

senses.definition: To exchange text or voice messages in real time through a computer network such as a social media chat room or messaging application.
senses.example: Do you want to chat online later?

senses.definition: To chat shit (to speak nonsense, to lie).
senses.example: Don't listen to me, I'm chatting.

senses.definition: To use ChatGPT to perform a task. (Can we verify this sense?)
An exchange of text or voice messages in real time through a computer network, resembling a face-to-face conversation.
senses.example: Internet Relay Chat

senses.definition: Informal conversation.
senses.example: It'd be cool to meet up again soon and have a quick chat.

senses.definition: A chat room, especially (in later use) one accompanying a videoconference or live stream.
senses.example: "Type yes in (the) chat if you can hear me."

senses.definition: The entirety of users, viewed collectively, in a chat room, especially the chat room accompanying a live stream.
senses.example: The chat just made a joke about my poor skillz.

senses.definition: Familiar term of address for users on social media other than a chat room, as in "guys."
Another term for ChatGPT.
Any of various small Old World passerine birds in the muscicapid tribe Saxicolini or subfamily Saxicolinae that feed on insects.
Any of several small Australian honeyeaters in the genus Epthianura.
A small potato, such as is given to swine.
Mining waste from lead and zinc mines.
A louse (small, parasitic insect).
Used to introduce a question, to address all the other people present.
senses.example: Chat, is this real?

core.definition: To talk in a friendly, informal way with someone, usually about everyday things.

pronunciation.tip: Say it with a short a as in 'cat' and a crisp final t. Do not stretch the vowel, and keep the t clear before a word like 'with'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests a relaxed, friendly exchange, though it can sound trivial if you want serious discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chat constantly in everyday speech for talking with coworkers, neighbors or friends about nothing in particular. It is informal, so avoid it in an interview or a formal meeting, where 'talk' or 'discuss' fits better. For text or website messaging, chat is the normal word, so a live chat with a support agent is a chat in the online sense. A natural reply to 'Let's chat later' is 'Sounds good.'

distinctions.note: Talk is the general word; chat means a relaxed, informal conversation, often without a clear purpose.
Discuss means to talk through a topic in detail, usually with a goal; chat is lighter and more casual.
Gossip means talking about other people's private lives, often unkindly; chat can be about anything.

examples.everyday: Hey, we should grab coffee sometime and chat about what's going on with your new job.
examples.professional: Can we chat for ten minutes after the stand-up about the data pipeline?
examples.analytical: Online chat has changed the rhythm of public argument, rewarding quick replies over careful, extended reasoning.

nuance.analogy: Like tossing a ball back and forth: light, quick, and not meant to end in a final score.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of quick, light talk; related to chatter, from Middle English chateren.
common_mistakes: Saying chat to someone, which sounds British; Americans say chat with someone.
Using chat for a formal discussion, as in 'we chatted the contract', which sounds odd; use discuss instead.

conversation.text: I chatted with Priya for a while at the coffee machine.
Do you have a minute? I'd love to have a quick chat.
Just send me the link in the chat during the call.

senses.definition: A situation in which an injury or other undesirable outcome is narrowly avoided.
senses.example: He had a close call when a truck ran a red light and almost hit him.

core.definition: A situation in which something bad, such as an accident or a serious mistake, almost happens but is narrowly avoided.

pronunciation.tip: Close here is the adjective, so the final s is voiceless and sounds like 's,' not 'z.' The vowel in call is the cot-caught sound, so say KAWL, not KAHL.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, often with relief. It describes danger or a mistake that did not happen, so it usually sounds lighter than 'disaster.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'that was a close call' after a near car accident, a near miss on a plane, or a nearly missed deadline. Common replies include 'Phew, that was close!' or 'Yeah, I thought we were done for.' It is very casual and safe for almost any conversation.

distinctions.note: Near miss often describes an event where two things almost collided, while close call is broader and can describe a mistake or a deadline.
Narrow escape sounds more literary or dramatic, while close call is the everyday American phrase.

examples.everyday: That truck almost hit us on the highway, so that was a close call.
examples.professional: We almost missed the release freeze, so it was a close call, but the deployment went through.
examples.analytical: The historical record shows several close calls in which a single decision avoided catastrophe, which makes the role of chance hard to ignore.

nuance.analogy: Like a dish sliding toward the edge of a table and stopping just before it falls.
nuance.etymology: Close comes from Latin clausus, shut, through Old French clos; call is from Old Norse kalla, to name or summon.
common_mistakes: Saying 'a close one' in formal writing, when 'close call' is the standard phrase.
Pronouncing close with a z sound, as in the verb, instead of the s sound of the adjective.

conversation.text: That truck almost hit us. That was a close call!
We fixed the server ten minutes before the demo; it was a close call.
It was a close call, but we caught the train.

senses.definition: In a confident manner; with confidence; with strong assurance; positively.
senses.example: Alice confidently stepped up on the platform to give her maiden speech as CEO.

core.definition: In a way that shows you believe strongly in yourself or in what you are doing or saying.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, KAHN. The middle syllables are reduced, and the -tly ending is often pronounced as a quick 'lee' sound, with the t often nearly silent. Avoid stressing the -dent syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests calm self-assurance and competence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use confidently often to describe how someone speaks, moves, or makes a decision, as in 'she answered confidently.' In casual speech people often say 'with confidence' or 'like they knew what they were doing.' Confidently is neutral and does not imply arrogance unless the context suggests it.

distinctions.note: Boldly suggests courage or daring, sometimes taking a risk; confidently suggests calm belief in your ability or the outcome.
Arrogantly implies an unpleasant sense of superiority; confidently is positive and does not imply that.

examples.everyday: She walked into the interview room confidently, even though she was nervous inside.
examples.professional: I can confidently say the model will meet the accuracy target once we retrain it with the new data.
examples.analytical: The author confidently asserts that faith can be known through reason, though he does not fully explain how.

nuance.analogy: Acting confidently is like walking across a sturdy bridge: you do not look down, because you trust it will hold.
nuance.etymology: From Latin confidere, to trust fully, from com- 'together' and fidere 'to trust'.
common_mistakes: Spelling it as 'confidentally,' which is incorrect.
Stressing the middle syllable 'den' instead of the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind 'confidence' in the New Testament is parrhēsia, meaning boldness, openness, or freedom of speech. Hebrews 4:16 in the RSV says believers should draw near to the throne of grace with confidence. 1 John 5:14 speaks of the confidence we have in God, that he hears us when we ask according to his will.

senses.definition: Complex, complicated, or intricate.
senses.example: He gave a convoluted explanation that amounted to little more than a weak excuse for his absence.

senses.definition: Having numerous overlapping coils or folds; convolute.

core.definition: Very complicated and hard to follow, with too many twists, details, or steps.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAHN-, not on the second. The final -ed is pronounced as 'id' in this word, and the middle vowels are weak.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually criticizes an explanation, plan, or argument for being unnecessarily complicated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word often in everyday speech and in workplace talk to complain about confusing rules, instructions, or stories. It is neutral in tone but usually implies a mild criticism. You might say 'That's a convoluted way to do it' when someone takes an overly complex route.

distinctions.note: Complicated is neutral and general, while convoluted suggests complexity that is unnecessary or hard to follow because of too many twists.
Complex can describe something sophisticated but well-organized, whereas convoluted usually implies tangled or confusing.

examples.everyday: Getting the refund took forever because the store's return process was so convoluted.
examples.professional: The approval workflow is too convoluted, so let's simplify it before we roll it out to the whole team.
examples.analytical: The author's argument becomes convoluted when he tries to reconcile two incompatible definitions of freedom.

nuance.analogy: A convoluted path is like a garden hose left in a knot: water can still get through, but only after a lot of untangling.
nuance.etymology: From Latin convolutus, past participle of convolvere, 'to roll together,' from con- 'together' and volvere 'to roll.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural.
Using it as a neutral synonym for 'complex' when you mean well-organized complexity.

senses.definition: A person to whom a debt is owed.
senses.example: The creditor demanded immediate payment.

senses.definition: One who gives credence to something; a believer.

core.definition: A person, bank, or company to whom money is owed and who has the right to be repaid.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KRED. The final -or is a reduced American 'er' sound, not 'or' as in 'door'. The t in the middle is a clear t, not a flap, because it comes before an unstressed vowel after a stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a role in a financial or legal relationship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use creditor mainly in finance, law, and business, especially in bankruptcy and collections. In everyday talk people say the bank, the lender, or the person I owe. In a bankruptcy or legal letter, you may see creditors used in the plural to mean everyone owed money.

distinctions.note: A creditor is the one owed money, while a debtor is the one who owes it.
A lender is a broader term for anyone who loans money; creditor emphasizes the legal right to be repaid.
Creditable means deserving praise or respect, and it is not the same as creditor.

examples.everyday: I owe the bank money, so the bank is my creditor.
examples.professional: Before the merger closes, the company must notify every creditor and secure their consent.
examples.analytical: In Luke's parable, the creditor forgives both debtors, and the question becomes which debtor loves him more.

nuance.analogy: A creditor is like the person holding the receipt for a loan: the debt exists because they trusted you with something first.
nuance.etymology: From Latin creditor, one who trusts or lends, from credere, to believe, trust.
common_mistakes: Confusing creditor with creditable, which describes something deserving praise.
Saying creditor with a strong 'or' ending instead of a reduced 'er' sound.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is danistēs, a moneylender or creditor. In Luke 7:41-43 the RSV describes a creditor with two debtors, one who owes much and one who owes little, and the creditor forgives both, illustrating God's grace and the response of love. In Matthew 18:23-35 the parable of the unforgiving servant uses the language of debt and forgiveness to teach that those who receive mercy must show mercy.

creditor.etymology: From Middle English *creditour*, from Anglo-Norman *creditour*, from Latin *crēditor*, from *crēditum* (“loan”), from *crēditus*, perfect passive participle of *crēdō* (“lend”).

senses.definition: Containing a dense pack or mass of something; teeming.

core.definition: Full of people or things packed closely together, leaving little free space.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: KROWD-ihd. The ow is a diphthong as in 'cloud', and the final -ed is a full syllable /ɪd/ because it is an adjective.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on whether the crowd is pleasant or uncomfortable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use crowded about streets, stores, trains, and events, often in complaints such as 'The store is so crowded today.' It is very common in casual speech. For a crowd at a party, lively is more positive, while crowded implies the space is uncomfortably full.

distinctions.note: Packed is more informal and stronger, suggesting no room at all, while crowded can describe a busy but still movable space.
Busy describes activity, while crowded describes the number of people or things taking up space.

examples.everyday: The mall is really crowded on Saturdays, so let's go in the morning.
examples.professional: The meeting room was too crowded, so we moved the team standup to the lounge.
examples.analytical: The crowded field of competing theories made it hard to identify any single dominant explanation.

nuance.analogy: A crowded room is like a bus at rush hour, with every seat taken and people standing close together.
nuance.etymology: From crowd, from Old English crūdan, to press, plus the adjective suffix -ed.
common_mistakes: Using crowded with a preposition other than with, as in 'crowded of people'.
Stressing the second syllable or pronouncing the -ed as a silent ending.

conversation.text: The beach was so crowded we could barely find a spot.
Let's go early before it gets crowded.
The pool is less crowded in the evening.

senses.definition: A record of where data came from and how it was processed.

core.definition: A recorded history showing where a dataset came from, who changed it, and what processing steps it went through.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable of 'provenance', PRAH. The second syllable is reduced to a schwa, and the final 'ance' is a weak 'uns'. Americans pronounce the r clearly and the first vowel like 'ah', as in 'top'.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It describes a verification practice and sounds precise and academic.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and engineers use this phrase when they need to trace the origin of training or analytical data, especially in regulated fields or research reproducibility. Americans say it mostly in professional or academic settings. In everyday talk, people would say 'where the data came from' instead.

distinctions.note: Data lineage tracks how data moves and transforms through systems, while data provenance focuses on the origin and authenticity of the original source.
Metadata is any descriptive information about data, whereas provenance is a specific kind of metadata about origin and history.
A data source is just the place data comes from; provenance adds the full record of how it was handled since then.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in journalism says her team checks data provenance before they publish any numbers from a government report.
examples.professional: Before we merge the vendor's survey results, can you document the data provenance so the audit team knows where each field came from?
examples.analytical: Without data provenance, a dataset loses its evidential weight, because a conclusion can only be as credible as the chain of custody that connects it to its source.

nuance.analogy: Like the chain of custody for evidence in a police investigation, which records every hand the item passed through.
nuance.etymology: 'Provenance' from French provenance, from Latin provenire, 'to come forth'.
common_mistakes: Using 'provenance' to mean only the original source; it also includes the processing history.
Misspelling it as 'providence', which means divine care or foresight.

conversation.text: Data provenance tracks where each piece of data came from and how it was processed.
Good data provenance lets us show we had the rights to use every dataset.
Without data provenance, we couldn't tell which scrape introduced the duplicates.

senses.definition: An area with no life.
An area of the ocean where oxygen levels are too low to support life, especially as a result of pollution.
A region where mobile phones do not operate because there is no base station or repeater nearby.
A region within the player's viewpoint that is less sensitive to small movements, aiding accurate firing of weapons etc.

The part of the field where a player is on their opponent's side of the field but kicking a field goal would probably be unsuccessful and punting the ball would not dramatically change field position.
An area near a fortification that is relatively sheltered from defending fire because direct fire from other parts of the walls cannot be directed around a curved wall.

core.definition: An area where mobile phones do not work because there is no nearby signal tower or repeater.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZOHN, the second word. Keep dead short and unstressed, and the final n should be clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It describes a practical inconvenience, usually when you are in a rural area, a building or a tunnel.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say I'm in a dead zone when a call drops in the mountains, a subway or a basement. In phone conversations, you can say Sorry, I'm in a dead zone, can you hear me now? A natural reply is Let me call you back when I get a signal.

distinctions.note: Dead spot is a similar term for a place with no signal, while dead zone is more common in phone and network contexts.
An ocean dead zone is a part of the sea with too little oxygen for life, so the term has a different meaning from a cell phone dead zone.

collocations: no signal in a dead zone

examples.everyday: Sorry, I'm in a dead zone, so I'll text you when I get home.
examples.professional: The call dropped because our conference room is a dead zone for the carrier, so please dial in from the hallway.
examples.analytical: Coverage maps often hide dead zones, which can leave rural communities without reliable emergency communication.

nuance.analogy: A dead zone is like a room with no Wi-Fi in a house: the signal is there nearby, but it does not reach that place.
nuance.etymology: Dead from Old English dead and zone from Greek zōnē, meaning belt or girdle, used for an area of defined extent.
common_mistakes: Saying dead zone as one word, since it is two words in standard American writing.
Confusing this with the ocean sense of dead zone in technical contexts.

conversation.text: This stretch of highway is a dead zone, so the call might drop.
My kitchen is a dead zone; I have to go upstairs to make calls.
We lost him in the dead zone near the tunnel.

senses.definition: In intuitionistic logic, a proposition P is decidable in a given theory if it can be proven from the theory that "either P or not P", i.e. in symbols: P∨¬P.
Capable of being decided.
Describing a set for which there exists an algorithm that will determine whether any element is or is not within the set in a finite amount of time.
senses.example: It is easy to show that the set of even numbers is decidable by creating the relevant Turing machine.

core.definition: Able to be settled by a clear rule or procedure, so that a definite yes-or-no answer can always be found.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, SY, and make the last two syllables weak: 'duh-bul.' Americans often say the final syllable as a very light 'bul,' so avoid giving it full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term and does not carry a positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, decidable is used mainly in logic, mathematics and computer science, especially to say whether a problem or statement has an algorithmic answer. In ordinary conversation people say 'can be decided' or 'can be settled' instead. The phrase 'decidable in a theory' is a technical use that appears in formal logic courses and papers.

distinctions.note: Decidable refers to a formal property of a problem, while open means no one has yet resolved the question, even though it might be decidable in principle.
Settled is an everyday word for a question that has been resolved, while decidable is a technical property of whether such resolution is possible by a method.

examples.everyday: Whether we stay in or go out tonight is decidable once we check the forecast.
examples.professional: The team asked whether the satisfiability problem for this fragment is decidable before choosing a solver.
examples.analytical: A proposition may be decidable in a given theory even when it is not decidable in pure logic, which shows how context shapes provability.

nuance.analogy: A decidable question is like a math problem with a recipe that always gives an answer, even if the recipe takes a while.
nuance.etymology: From Latin decidere, to cut off or settle, through decide.
common_mistakes: Saying decidable when you mean 'a decision that was made,' which is decided or decision.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable, as in DE-cidable, instead of dih-SY-duh-bul.

senses.definition: To unlink; to take apart or come apart.
senses.example: radiation decoupled from matter

senses.definition: To muffle the seismic waves of (a nuclear explosion) by performing it underground.

core.definition: Separated or disconnected so that one thing no longer depends on or affects another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'KUP'. The 'de-' is 'dee', not 'deck'. The ending '-led' is a reduced 'uld', and the word has only two stressed-syllable beats.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term in software and engineering.
nuance.usage_note: In American software and engineering teams, 'decouple' means separating parts so they can change independently. You will hear 'decouple the service' or 'decouple the deployment'. In everyday speech, people say 'separate', 'disconnect', or 'unlink'.

distinctions.note: 'Separated' is general and everyday; 'decoupled' specifically means removing a dependency between systems or parts.
'Disconnected' usually refers to physical links or networks; 'decoupled' refers to logical or structural dependency.

examples.everyday: My phone and my watch are decoupled now, so I can use each one separately.
examples.professional: We decoupled the payment service from the order system so each team can deploy on its own schedule.
examples.analytical: A central claim of the essay is that moral reasoning can be decoupled from religious authority without losing its substance.

nuance.analogy: Decoupling is like unhooking a trailer from a truck: each can move without dragging the other.
nuance.etymology: From de- 'reverse' plus couple, from Latin copula, 'bond'.
common_mistakes: Using the spelling 'decoupled' with a long 'oo' sound; the first vowel is 'ee'.
Using it in everyday speech where 'separate' is clearer.

senses.definition: The representation of objects anew, in a way that we do not recognize, or that changes our reading of them.

core.definition: A literary technique of presenting familiar things in a strange way so readers see them freshly and notice what habit had hidden.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on ZAY, near the end, with secondary stress on 'dee'. Don't reduce the 'ee' in 'mil-yuh' too much; say 'mil-yuh' smoothly, with the r in 'ruh' clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a deliberate artistic method, usually praised in literary criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use defamiliarization almost only in literary criticism, theory, and university courses. It is not an everyday word. In conversation, people would more likely say 'seeing something in a new way' or 'making the familiar strange'. The term is most natural in academic writing or when discussing Russian Formalism or modernist fiction.

distinctions.note: Estrangement is a broader term for a sense of alienation, while defamiliarization is a specific technique used in art.
Alienation often describes a social or emotional state, whereas defamiliarization describes an artistic method that makes the reader notice.

examples.everyday: My book club argued about whether that author's strange descriptions were just confusing or a kind of defamiliarization.
examples.professional: In the workshop, we used defamiliarization to help our writers describe their office in a way that surprised readers.
examples.analytical: Shklovsky argued that defamiliarization restores our perception of the world by making ordinary objects appear unfamiliar.

nuance.analogy: Like seeing your own living room through the eyes of a visitor from another country, noticing details you no longer see.
nuance.etymology: Coined from 'de-' (away from), 'familiar', and '-ization', from Russian 'ostranenie' as translated by Viktor Shklovsky's theory.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'defamation', which is a legal term about harming reputation.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'dee-fuh-mil-ee-uh-ruh-ZAY-shun' with an extra vowel.

senses.definition: The act of setting free or extricating from danger, imprisonment, bondage, evil, etc.
The act of delivering or conveying something.
Delivery in childbirth.

core.definition: The act of rescuing or freeing someone or something from danger, captivity, evil, or harm.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on LIV. The middle syllable is a weak American 'er', and the final -ance is a soft 'uns', not 'ahnss'.

nuance.connotation: positive
nuance.usage_note: Americans use deliverance mainly in religious, literary, or formal speech, such as sermons, hymns, and prayers. In everyday talk people would say rescue, relief, or getting out of trouble. Saying you prayed for deliverance is natural in church settings.

distinctions.note: Rescue is the everyday word for saving someone from immediate danger, while deliverance often implies a larger, sometimes spiritual or long-awaited freedom.
Salvation in Christian use refers to being saved from sin and its consequences, while deliverance more often means freedom from a particular danger, enemy, or affliction.

examples.everyday: After the flood waters finally went down, we felt a huge sense of deliverance when the power came back on.
examples.professional: In the sermon for the leadership retreat, the speaker described the team's escape from the failed project as a kind of deliverance.
examples.analytical: The psalmist's cries for deliverance assume a God who hears and acts, which shapes how the whole lament is read.

nuance.analogy: Deliverance is like a rope thrown to someone who is drowning: it is the moment the danger ends and they are pulled to safety.
nuance.etymology: From deliver (Latin liberare, to set free) plus -ance, the state or act of being freed.
common_mistakes: Confusing deliverance with delivery, which usually means the act of bringing goods or a baby.
Stressing the last syllable as in dih-liv-er-ANCE.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the idea of deliverance translates several concepts. The Hebrew word yashaʿ (to save, to deliver) is used of God rescuing Israel from enemies and oppression, and the Greek verb rhyomai (to rescue, to deliver) appears in the Lord's Prayer. Psalm 34:4 describes the LORD answering the psalmist and delivering him from all his fears. Exodus 14:30 says the LORD saved Israel from the Egyptians that day, showing deliverance as God's act on behalf of his people. Matthew 6:13 asks God to deliver us from evil, which connects deliverance to protection from spiritual danger.

senses.definition: The act or process of denormalizing.

core.definition: In database design, adding redundant data to a normalized database to speed up reading or querying it.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on ZAY, and the secondary stress is on the first syllable, dee. Pronounce the -ization ending as 'ih-ZAY-shun', with a reduced middle vowel.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use denormalization in software engineering, database administration and data science, mainly in design discussions. It is a technical term, so people say it when deciding how to trade storage or consistency for speed. In casual talk, one would just say 'copying the data into the table'.

distinctions.note: Normalization removes redundancy to protect data integrity, while denormalization deliberately adds redundancy for performance.
Duplication is a general term for copying data, while denormalization is a deliberate design decision in a schema.

examples.everyday: Our app loads slowly, so the team is talking about denormalization to speed up the user profile page.
examples.professional: Denormalization made the dashboard queries much faster, but we now need a process to keep the duplicate fields in sync.
examples.analytical: The argument for denormalization depends on a trade-off between data integrity and read performance that the design document does not fully specify.

nuance.analogy: Denormalization is like keeping a copy of a friend's phone number in several notebooks: it is faster to find, but you must update every copy when it changes.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from de- (reversal) and normalization, from the Latin norma, 'carpenter's square, rule'.
common_mistakes: Using denormalization to mean any messy or unstructured data, when it is a specific design choice.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'dee-NOR-muh-liz-ay-shun'.

senses.definition: In a detached manner.

core.definition: In a calm, distant way that shows no personal emotion or involvement.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TACH. The -ed here is a separate syllable, 'id', because it comes before the -ly ending, so the word has four syllables.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It suggests calm distance, which may read as coldness or objectivity depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use detachedly mostly in writing, especially in criticism, fiction, or analysis, to describe how someone speaks or observes. It is less common in speech, where people more often say 'coolly' or 'with no emotion'. The word is correct but sounds learned, so use it when precision matters.

distinctions.note: Coolly suggests calm or even unfriendly behavior, while detachedly focuses on a lack of personal involvement or emotion.
Objectively describes fair judgment based on facts, while detachedly describes an emotional distance that may or may not be fair.

examples.everyday: She listened to the complaint detachedly, as if it had nothing to do with her.
examples.professional: The reviewer wrote detachedly about the product, without mentioning how users actually felt.
examples.analytical: The narrator recounts the war detachedly, which makes the violence feel more disturbing rather than less.

nuance.analogy: Speaking detachedly is like reading a weather report: the information is clear, but the speaker is not personally affected.
nuance.etymology: From detached, past participle of detach, plus the adverb ending -ly.
common_mistakes: Using detachedly for a physical separation; it describes manner, not physical state.
Pronouncing the -ed as silent and dropping the middle syllable.

senses.definition: Being of the second canon of the Old Testament of the Bible, and not accepted by some Christians. Part of the Apocrypha.
Of, within, or according to a decidedly lesser canon of installments in a franchise.

core.definition: Describing the Old Testament books accepted by Catholics and Orthodox as Scripture but not found in the Hebrew Bible or Protestant canon.

pronunciation.tip: Main stress on NAH, with secondary stress on the first syllable 'doo'. Say 'doo', not 'dyoo'. The r is clearly pronounced before the oh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, technical.
nuance.usage_note: Used mainly by Catholic and academic writers. Protestants usually say 'Apocrypha' for the same books. Use it carefully to avoid taking sides.

distinctions.note: Apocryphal suggests doubtful status; deuterocanonical affirms the books are canonical.
Protocanonical books were accepted early and widely; deuterocanonical were accepted later or disputed.
Noncanonical means outside any canon; deuterocanonical are within the Catholic and Orthodox canons.

examples.everyday: My Catholic friend showed me that her Bible includes Tobit and other deuterocanonical books.
examples.professional: The seminar compared how Catholic and Protestant editions handle the deuterocanonical books.
examples.analytical: The deuterocanonical books, transmitted in the Septuagint, shaped early Christian reading of the Old Testament.

nuance.analogy: Like a second set of chapters added to an official list, 'second canon' as the Greek suggests.
nuance.etymology: From Greek deuteros, 'second' + canonical, 'belonging to the canon'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'dyoo-' instead of 'doo-'.
Using it as a synonym for 'fake' or 'apocryphal'.
Misplacing stress on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: These books include Tobit, Judith, Wisdom of Solomon, Sirach, Baruch, 1-2 Maccabees, and additions to Esther and Daniel. They appear in the Septuagint, which many early Christians used.

traditions.view: These books are received as Scripture and read in worship, though the Orthodox canon includes some others and the list varies slightly.
They are fully canonical and inspired, defined at Trent, though 'deuterocanonical' marks their later general acceptance.
Protestants usually call them Apocrypha and exclude them from the canon; Lutherans and Anglicans allow them for edification but not doctrine.

senses.definition: To give one's time, focus one's efforts, commit oneself, etc. entirely for, on, or to a certain matter; to consecrate.
senses.example: They devoted their lives to following Jesus Christ.

senses.definition: To consign over; to doom.
senses.example: to devote one to destruction

senses.definition: To execrate; to curse.

core.definition: To give time, energy, or attention entirely to a purpose, activity, or person.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the vowel is a long 'oh' that glides to 'oo'. The final 't' is a clear stop, not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests commitment, dedication, and sacrifice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say devote time to, devote energy to, or devote yourself to something. It is common in writing, speeches, and self-description, and sounds slightly formal in casual talk where people say spend or put into. Be sure to use a preposition after it.

distinctions.note: Spend is neutral and everyday; devote suggests dedicating time or effort on purpose toward a cause.
Dedicate is close in meaning but often used for a formal, ceremonial, or public commitment.

examples.everyday: I want to devote more weekends to hiking this summer.
examples.professional: We should devote the next sprint to fixing the data pipeline.
examples.analytical: Augustine devotes much of the Confessions to examining how the soul turns toward God.

nuance.analogy: To devote yourself to something is like pointing a flashlight steadily at one spot on a dark path, letting everything else fade.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'devovere', meaning to vow or consecrate, from 'de-' (down) and 'vovere' (to vow).
common_mistakes: Omitting the preposition: say devote time to, not devote time.
Confusing devote with devoted when using it as a verb in a sentence.

devote.etymology: Latin *dēvōtus*, past participle of Latin *dēvoveō* (“dedicate by a vow, sacrifice oneself, promise solemnly”). see also *devout*.

senses.definition: A methodical inquiry or investigation.
A lengthy, formal discourse that analyses or explains some topic; a dissertation or treatise.

core.definition: A long, detailed, formal essay or talk that explains a subject thoroughly.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on -ZISH-, and the second syllable -kwuh- is reduced. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce the middle sound as 'kwah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes a long, sometimes tedious, discourse that can seem overly detailed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disquisition in academic writing, reviews, and literary criticism. It is rarely used in everyday talk. If you describe a speech as a disquisition, you are saying it was long and thorough, sometimes too much so. In casual conversation say a long explanation or a lecture.

distinctions.note: A dissertation is a formal academic work, often a doctoral thesis, while disquisition is a broader term for any detailed formal discourse.
A lecture is an oral presentation for students or an audience. A disquisition can be written or spoken and is typically more formal and extended.

examples.everyday: My professor gave us a long disquisition on the causes of the Civil War, and I got lost halfway through.
examples.professional: The design document includes a disquisition on why we chose event sourcing, which is more than most people will read.
examples.analytical: Kant's disquisition on the limits of reason sets the terms for much of later epistemology.

nuance.analogy: A disquisition is like a long, carefully built bridge of argument, where each section supports the next and carries the reader across the whole subject.
nuance.etymology: From Latin disquisitio, from disquirere, to inquire thoroughly.
common_mistakes: Using disquisition for a short remark; it implies a long, formal treatment.
Confusing it with inquisition, which refers to a formal investigation or, historically, the Inquisition.

disquisition.etymology: Borrowed from French *disquisition* (“disquisition”), from Latin *disquīsītiō* (“inquiry, investigation”), from *disquīrō* (“to investigate”) (from *dis-* + *quaerō* (“to look for, seek; to inquire, question”)) + *-tiō*.

senses.definition: A physician; a member of the medical profession; one who is trained and licensed to heal the sick or injured. The final examination and qualification may award a doctor degree in which case the post-nominal letters are DO, DPM, MD, DMD, or DDS in the US, or MBBS or BDS in the UK.
senses.example: If you still feel unwell tomorrow, see your doctor.

senses.definition: A person who has attained a doctorate, such as a Ph.D. or Th.D. or one of many other terminal degrees conferred by a college or university.
A veterinarian; a medical practitioner who treats non-human animals.
A nickname for a person who has special knowledge or talents to manipulate or arrange transactions.
A fish, the friar skate.
Any mechanical contrivance intended to remedy a difficulty or serve some purpose in an exigency.
senses.example: the doctor of a calico-printing machine, which is a knife to remove superfluous coloring matter

senses.definition: To act as a medical doctor to.
senses.example: Her children doctored her back to health.

senses.definition: To act as a medical doctor.
To make (someone) into an (academic) doctor; to confer a doctorate upon.
To physically alter (medically or surgically) a living being in order to change growth or behavior.
senses.example: They doctored their apple trees by vigorous pruning, and now the dwarfed trees are easier to pick.

senses.definition: To genetically alter an extant species.
senses.example: Mendel's discoveries showed how the evolution of a species may be doctored.

senses.definition: To alter or make obscure, as with the intention to deceive, especially a document.
senses.example: To doctor the signature of an instrument with intent to defraud is an example of forgery.

senses.definition: To adulterate, drug, or poison (drink).

core.definition: A person who is trained and licensed to diagnose and treat illness or injury, usually a physician.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, DAHK. The final syllable is an American r-colored er, not a full oar, and the t is a clear t, not a flap, because it comes before a stressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and respectful; the word carries trust and authority.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, doctor usually means a medical doctor, and people say I'm seeing my doctor or I need to call the doctor's office. Americans also use Doctor for holders of a PhD or other doctorate, such as Dr. Smith in a university setting, so context matters. In a medical setting, the title Dr. is used in front of a surname, and patients often address a doctor as Doctor.

distinctions.note: Physician is the more formal term for a medical doctor, while doctor is the everyday word used by most people.
A nurse provides care under a doctor's direction, but a doctor has more training and makes diagnoses and treatment decisions.

examples.everyday: I need to see a doctor about this cough because it has lasted three weeks.
examples.professional: Dr. Patel, who holds a doctorate in statistics, leads our analytics group and reviews every model before launch.
examples.analytical: A doctor's authority in the clinic rests on licensure, training, and institutional trust, not only on expertise.

nuance.analogy: A doctor is like a mechanic for the human body: trained to find what is wrong, fix it, and explain the repair.
nuance.etymology: From Latin doctor, teacher, from docere, to teach.
common_mistakes: Using doctor for every medical worker; in American usage, nurses and physician assistants are not doctors.
Saying doctor with a flapped t in the middle, but the t before a stressed syllable should be a clear t.

doctor.etymology: From Middle English *doctor*, *doctour* (“an expert, authority on a subject”), from Anglo-Norman *doctour*, from Latin *doctor* (“teacher”), from *doceō* (“to teach”).

conversation.text: I have a doctor's appointment at ten, so I'll be late.
You should see a doctor if the cough doesn't go away.
My doctor told me to drink more water and get more sleep.

senses.definition: The sediment settled at the bottom of a liquid; the lees in a container of unfiltered wine.
The worst and lowest part of something.
senses.example: the dregs of society

core.definition: The sediment at the bottom of a liquid, or the worst and least valuable part of something.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with a short 'e' as in 'bed'. The final sound is a voiced 'z', and it is always plural in form.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it refers to leftover or worst portions, often with a sense of decline.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'dregs' mostly in the phrase 'the dregs of society' or 'drink to the dregs'. For coffee or wine, people say 'grounds' or 'sediment' in everyday speech. The word is used in a figurative sense more often than literally.

distinctions.note: 'Sediment' is the technical or general word for settled material in a liquid; 'dregs' is more poetic and often figurative.
'Grounds' is the everyday American word for coffee residue; 'dregs' is more literary.

examples.everyday: Pour the coffee slowly so you don't get the dregs at the bottom.
examples.professional: The company hired the dregs of the job market because it had no budget for experienced staff.
examples.analytical: The novelist portrays the city's political class as the dregs of a corrupt system.

nuance.analogy: Like the last few spoonfuls of muddy sediment at the bottom of a glass of wine, left after the good part is poured out.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English 'dreg', from Old Norse 'dregg', meaning sediment or lees.
common_mistakes: Using 'dregs' as singular; it is normally plural.
Pronouncing the final sound as 's' instead of a voiced 'z'.

senses.definition: Short for clothes dryer, tumble dryer.
Short for hair dryer.
One who, or that which, dries; any device or facility employed to remove water or humidity, e.g. a desiccative.
senses.example: The sun and a northwesterly wind are great driers of the earth.

senses.definition: A catalyst used to promote the drying of paints and varnishes by oxidative crosslinking.

core.definition: A machine that removes moisture from clothes or hair, most often a clothes dryer or hair dryer.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce the first syllable with a long i and an American rhotic r, and the second syllable as a reduced, unstressed 'er'. Do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often mean the clothes dryer when they say 'dryer' alone, so 'Put it in the dryer' is standard. In a bathroom or salon context, say 'hair dryer'. The British 'tumble dryer' is rarely used in American speech.

distinctions.note: Drier is the comparative of dry (more dry); dryer is the appliance. Americans also sometimes spell the comparative 'drier', so both are accepted for the adjective.
A dehumidifier removes moisture from air in a room; a dryer removes moisture from objects like clothes or hair.

examples.everyday: Can you move your jacket out of the dryer? It's done.
examples.professional: The dryer in the lab is running hot, so we should check the thermostat before loading the next batch.
examples.analytical: A desiccant dryer removes water vapor from a gas stream by adsorption, so its performance depends on the regeneration cycle.

nuance.analogy: A dryer works like a sunny day, pulling water out of wet things in a closed drum.
nuance.etymology: From 'dry' (Old English 'drȳge') with the agent suffix '-er'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'drier' for the appliance; the standard American word is 'dryer'.
Saying 'tumble dryer', which sounds British in American speech.

dryer.etymology: From Middle English *driere*, *dreyere* (“one who dries”), equivalent to *dry* + *-er*.

conversation.text: Don't put my sweater in the dryer; it'll shrink.
The dryer takes forever, so I hang some things up.
Can I borrow your hair dryer? Mine just died.

senses.definition: Calm, relaxed, casual and informal.
Unhurried.

core.definition: Relaxed and calm, not easily upset, and happy to go along with plans or other people.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'GOH', and 'EE-zee' has a lighter secondary stress. Say 'goh-ing' with a clear 'oh' and a soft 'ing', not 'go-ing' as two separate words.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes someone who is pleasant and flexible, though it can sound lazy if overused.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use easygoing to describe a relaxed person, such as a roommate, coworker or boss, who does not make a fuss. It is common in casual talk and in describing personalities in job or dating conversations. A natural reply is 'Oh, good, I'm pretty easygoing too' or 'That sounds like a good fit.'

distinctions.note: Laid-back is very casual and sometimes implies lacking energy; easygoing is more positive and suggests flexibility.
Relaxed describes a state at a moment; easygoing describes a lasting personality trait.

examples.everyday: My new roommate is really easygoing, so we never argue about the dishes.
examples.professional: Our new manager is easygoing in meetings, but she keeps the deadlines firm.
examples.analytical: The Stoic ideal of an easygoing acceptance of events depends on distinguishing what is within our control.

nuance.analogy: Like a comfortable pair of old jeans that fits almost any situation.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, 'easy going', in formal writing where one word is standard.
Stressing 'easy' most strongly, which makes the word sound like 'EE-zee-go-ing' with flat stress.

conversation.text: My boss is pretty easygoing, so it's a nice place to work.
He's super easygoing; he's fine with whatever restaurant we pick.
She's easygoing about most things, but she hates being late.

senses.definition: The cardinal number immediately following eighty-three and preceding eighty-five.

core.definition: The cardinal number 84, one more than eighty-three and one less than eighty-five.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FOHR, and the r is pronounced clearly in American English. Do not drop the r or pronounce it like 'fore' in British style.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a plain number, often used for ages or Scripture references.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use eighty-four for ages, years, counts and scripture or page numbers. In speech it is often shortened casually, but full forms are standard in writing. It is also common in phrases like 'eighty-four years' when describing a lifespan.

distinctions.note: Fourteen stresses FOR-teen, while eighty-four stresses the final FOR of the number, so listeners can confuse them in fast speech. Listen for the -ty ending.

examples.everyday: Aunt Lorraine is eighty-four, and she still bakes pies for the whole church every Sunday.
examples.professional: The model reached eighty-four percent accuracy on the validation set after the third tuning pass.
examples.analytical: Eighty-four factors as two squared times three times seven, which makes it a useful example of a composite number.

nuance.analogy: Think of eighty-four as a stop on a train line that always comes right before eighty-five.
nuance.etymology: Formed from eighty plus four; eighty comes from Old English 'eahtatig', meaning eight tens.
common_mistakes: Dropping the final r, which makes the word sound like 'eighty-fo'.
Confusing it with fourteen when a speaker is reading numbers quickly.

senses.definition: An ancient region east of Mesopotamia, in what is now southwestern Iran, and the name of a son of Shem and of several biblical men.

core.definition: An ancient region east of Mesopotamia, in what is now southwestern Iran, and the name of a son of Shem and of several biblical men.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced 'um', so the name sounds like 'Ee-lum', not 'Ee-lahm'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a historical and biblical name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often meet Elam in Bible study, history, and archaeology. It is a proper noun and is used when discussing the ancient kingdom or Genesis genealogies. In casual speech it would be unfamiliar to most people unless they are discussing the Bible.

distinctions.note: Elah is a valley and a king in Judah and Israel. Elam is a large kingdom to the east, and the names are easy to confuse.

examples.everyday: I was reading about Elam in Genesis, and it's interesting that it was an actual kingdom in what is now Iran.
examples.professional: In the archaeology seminar, the presenter described Elam as one of the oldest urban civilizations in the Iranian plateau.
examples.analytical: Isaiah's oracles against Elam reflect the prophetic claim that Yahweh governs the nations, including those beyond Israel's borders.

nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Elam, the name of a son of Shem and of the region the Elamites inhabited.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the name with a long 'ah' vowel, 'EE-lahm'.
Confusing Elam with Elah, the valley where David fought Goliath.
nuance.biblical_note: Elam in Hebrew names a son of Shem in Genesis 10:22 and an ancient people and region east of Babylon. In Genesis 10:22, Elam is listed among the sons of Shem in the table of nations. In Isaiah 21:2, the prophet speaks of the troubles coming on Elam and Media. In Jeremiah 49:34-39, the prophet proclaims a message against Elam, showing that Yahweh judges nations beyond Israel.

senses.definition: In the Bible, a leader of the tribe of Reuben during the wilderness wanderings, son of Shedeur, who helped count the tribe in the census.

core.definition: In the Bible, a leader of the tribe of Reuben during the wilderness wanderings, son of Shedeur, who helped count the tribe in the census.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LY, which carries the long I sound. The last syllable is a reduced r-colored vowel, so say -zur.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a rare name, used mainly in religious or scholarly contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Elizur is almost never used as a personal name in the United States. Most Americans would only meet it in Bible study or reading about the book of Numbers. Speaking of him is simple and neutral.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study group we talked about Elizur, the Reuben leader who appears in the census lists.
examples.professional: The seminary handout listed Elizur among the tribal princes who assisted with the wilderness census.
examples.analytical: The census lists in Numbers identify Elizur as the representative of Reuben, which signals the importance of tribal leadership in Israel's organization.

nuance.analogy: Elizur is like a name on an official roster: short and specific, marking one person's role in a larger organization.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew Eliżur, meaning my God is a rock.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in EL-ih-zur.
Confusing him with Elizabeth, which is a different name for a different person.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew name Elitzur means God is a rock. Elizur appears as a prince of the tribe of Reuben. Numbers 1:5 names him as the son of Shedeur who helps count the tribe at Sinai. Numbers 2:10 places him as the leader of Reuben's camp on the south side. Numbers 7:30-35 describes his offering at the dedication of the altar.

senses.definition: A closed curve, the locus of a point such that the sum of the distances from that point to two other fixed points (called the foci of the ellipse) is constant; equivalently, the conic section that is the intersection of a cone with a plane that does not intersect the base of the cone.
To remove from a phrase a word which is grammatically needed, but which is clearly understood without having to be stated.
senses.example: In B's response to A's question:- (A: Would you like to go out?, B: I'd love to), the words that are ellipsed are go out.

core.definition: A closed oval curve in which the sum of the distances from any point on it to two fixed points, called foci, is constant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LIPS, which is a single syllable. Do not add a vowel between the p and s, and do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term in mathematics, science, and engineering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ellipse mainly in math, physics, astronomy, and design. In everyday speech they would say oval for a casual shape, though a planet's orbit is correctly called an ellipse. In a geometry class, the word is standard, and in grammar, the related word ellipsis has a different meaning.

distinctions.note: An oval is any egg-shaped or rounded closed curve, often without precise definition. An ellipse has an exact mathematical definition using two foci.
A circle is an ellipse with both foci at the same point. An ellipse has two distinct foci.

collocations: the major axis of an ellipse

examples.everyday: The track at the high school is shaped like an ellipse, so the runners go around the curves.
examples.professional: We modeled the satellite's path as an ellipse, so the team could estimate its closest and farthest distances from Earth.
examples.analytical: Kepler's first law states that each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, which challenged the older assumption of perfect circles.

nuance.analogy: An ellipse is like a circle stretched sideways, with two pins holding a loop of string around the sides.
nuance.etymology: From Greek elleipsis, a falling short or omission.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in EL-ips.
Using ellipse as a casual synonym for oval in everyday speech.

senses.definition: Identification with or understanding of the thoughts, feelings, or emotional state of another person.
senses.example: She had a lot of empathy for her neighbor; she knew what it was like to lose a parent too.

senses.definition: The capacity to understand another person's point of view or the result of such understanding.
A paranormal ability to psychically read another person's emotions.

core.definition: The ability to understand and share another person's feelings or point of view, especially when they are going through something difficult.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'th' is voiceless, as in 'thin', not 't' or 'd', and the final -y sounds like a short 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It is a valued quality in friends, leaders and counselors, though it can be used neutrally in academic discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use empathy often in everyday conversation, workplace talk and therapy settings, and it is widely praised. People usually say 'I have empathy for' or 'show empathy toward' someone. In casual talk, 'I feel for you' or 'I get it' can express the same idea more warmly.

distinctions.note: Sympathy means feeling sorry for someone or caring about their situation, while empathy means actually sharing or imagining their feelings from inside their experience.
Pity is a feeling of sorrow from a distance and can sound condescending, whereas empathy is an active understanding that treats the other person as an equal.

examples.everyday: My sister really listened when I told her I'd lost my job, and I could tell she had real empathy for what I was going through.
examples.professional: Good managers show empathy for their team when a deadline slips, but they still hold people accountable for the work.
examples.analytical: Edith Stein's phenomenological account treats empathy as the way we grasp another mind as other, without merging with it.

nuance.analogy: Empathy is like putting on someone else's shoes for a while, feeling where they pinch without pretending the shoes are yours.
nuance.etymology: From Greek empatheia, 'passion' or 'affection', from en- 'in' and pathos 'feeling'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'EM-path-ee' with the stress on the wrong syllable or pronouncing the 'th' as a 't'.
Using empathy to mean sympathy or pity, which makes the sentence sound like you feel sorry for someone rather than understanding them.

empathy.etymology: A 20th-century borrowing from Ancient Greek *ἐμπάθεια* (formed from *ἐν* (“in, at”) + *πάθος* (“feeling”)), equivalent to *em-* + *-pathy*, to translate German *Einfühlung*.

senses.definition: To continue or carry on, despite obstacles or hardships; to persist.
senses.example: The singer's popularity endured for decades.

senses.definition: To tolerate or put up with something unpleasant.
To last.
senses.example: Our love will endure forever.

senses.definition: To remain firm, as under trial or suffering; to suffer patiently or without yielding; to bear up under adversity; to hold out.
To suffer patiently.
senses.example: He endured years of pain.

core.definition: To keep going through something painful or difficult without giving up, or to put up with an unpleasant situation until it ends.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final r is pronounced clearly. Don't add an extra syllable at the end; the word is one syllable after the stress, not two.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. Enduring suffering is admired, but endure can also describe simply tolerating something boring or annoying, which is a mildly negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use endure for hardship, pain, grief, or long difficult periods, such as enduring a rough winter or a hard year at work. In casual speech people often say 'put up with' or 'deal with' instead, and 'I can't stand it' is more emotional. Endure sounds slightly formal or serious in everyday talk, so it fits well in speeches, sermons, and stories.

distinctions.note: Tolerate suggests accepting something you dislike without strong reaction; endure implies a longer or harder struggle.
Survive means to stay alive or continue existing after a danger; endure focuses on the experience of suffering through something.
Persist emphasizes continuing to try or to exist despite resistance; endure emphasizes bearing pain or hardship patiently.

examples.everyday: We had a terrible flight, but we managed to endure the delay with a few good movies.
examples.professional: Our team had to endure three months of database outages, but we finally finished the migration.
examples.analytical: The Psalmist teaches that the faithful can endure suffering because God remains present in the midst of it.

nuance.analogy: Like a bridge that holds up under heavy traffic year after year, a person who endures keeps bearing the weight without collapsing.
nuance.etymology: From Old French endurer, from Latin indurare, 'to harden,' from durus, 'hard.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'endure to' a noun without thinking; use 'endure' directly with the object, as in 'endure the pain'.
Confusing endure with ensure, which means to make certain something happens.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, endurance is a key virtue of faith. The Greek word hypomenō means 'to remain under, to bear up under, to persevere.' Romans 5:3-4 says suffering produces endurance, which produces character and hope. James 1:12 blesses the man who endures trial. Hebrews 12:7 tells believers to endure discipline as God's training.

endure.etymology: From Middle English *enduren*, from Old French *endurer*, from Latin *indūrō* (“to make hard”).

senses.definition: All of that part of a classical temple above the capitals of the columns; includes the architrave, frieze, and cornice but not the roof.

core.definition: In classical architecture, the horizontal structure resting on top of the columns, including the architrave, frieze, and cornice.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable of the stressed pair, en-TAB-, and the last syllables are reduced, so say -luh-chur quickly. Do not give each syllable equal weight.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise architectural term used in art history, architecture, and classical studies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use entablature mostly in architecture, art history, and classical studies, and in museum or heritage contexts. It is not a word for everyday conversation. When speaking about a building, people often say the decorated band above the columns or simply point to it.

distinctions.note: The architrave is only the lowest band of the entablature, resting directly on the columns, while entablature names the whole upper structure.
A cornice is the projecting top molding of an entablature or a wall, so it is one part of the entablature rather than the whole.

examples.everyday: When we toured the old courthouse, the guide pointed out the carved entablature above the columns.
examples.professional: The restoration contractor replaced the cracked stone in the entablature before the roof work began.
