examples.analytical: The Doric entablature divides horizontally into architrave, frieze, and cornice, expressing the classical ideal of proportion.

nuance.analogy: The entablature is like the horizontal beam and trim across the top of a door frame, but on a much larger classical scale.
nuance.etymology: From Italian entablatura, from the Italian verb intavolare, to set on a table or board.
common_mistakes: Confusing entablature with architrave, which is only one part of it.
Stressing the middle syllable, saying en-tuh-BLA-chur, rather than the first stressed syllable.

senses.definition: The embodiment or encapsulation of a class of items.
A representative example.
The height; the best; the most vivid.
A brief summary.

core.definition: A perfect example or embodiment of a quality, type or class of things.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable (PIT). The first and last syllables are reduced, so the word sounds like 'ih-PIT-uh-mee', not 'ih-PIT-oh-mee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises someone or something as the best or most typical example, though it can be used neutrally for a bad quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use epitome often in everyday praise, as in 'She's the epitome of grace.' It can also describe a negative quality, as in 'He's the epitome of rudeness.' It is common in both speech and writing, though a little formal for very casual talk.

distinctions.note: An example is any instance of something, while an epitome is the best or most complete example of it.
A model is a standard to imitate, while an epitome is an embodiment of a quality that already exists.

examples.everyday: She's the epitome of calm when the kids are screaming.
examples.professional: This dashboard is the epitome of clean design, so the executives can find the key numbers in seconds.
examples.analytical: The Gothic cathedral is the epitome of medieval architectural ambition, with its soaring vaults and light-filled windows.

nuance.analogy: An epitome is like a photo that captures the whole personality of its subject in one frame.
nuance.etymology: From Greek epitomē, 'a cutting short' or 'abridgment', from epitemnein 'to cut short'.
common_mistakes: Using 'epitome to' or 'epitome for' instead of 'the epitome of'.
Stressing the last syllable or pronouncing it as 'ih-PIT-oh-mee'.

epitome.etymology: From Middle French, from Latin *epitomē*, from Ancient Greek *ἐπιτομή* (“an abridgment, also a surface-incision”), from *ἐπιτέμνω* (“to cut upon the surface, cut short, abridge”), from *ἐπι-* + *τέμνω*.

senses.definition: An inclination to escape from routine or reality into fantasy.
A genre of book, film etc. that one uses to indulge this tendency.
The performance of an escape artist.

core.definition: The habit of mentally escaping from stress, boredom, or reality through fantasy, entertainment, or daydreaming.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the second syllable, 'skayp'. The final syllables are weak, so the 'ih' and 'um' vowels are reduced; avoid pronouncing the 'e' in 'escape' as 'ess'.

nuance.connotation: Usually neutral to mildly negative, implying avoidance of real problems. It can be positive when describing harmless relaxation, such as enjoying a novel after a hard day.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'escapism' in conversation about movies, books, video games, or vacation habits, often in a light, self-aware way: 'Honestly, I watch crime shows for escapism.' It becomes more critical when used of someone who avoids responsibilities. A natural reply is 'I hear you, sometimes you just need a break.'

distinctions.note: 'Escape' is the act of getting away, while 'escapism' is a habitual mental pattern of seeking fantasy to avoid reality.
A fantasy is an imagined scenario or a genre, while escapism describes the motive for seeking it out.

examples.everyday: I know it's silly, but I binge fantasy shows for pure escapism after work.
examples.professional: Some people treat the weekend as escapism from work, but I think we should address the real workload problems.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the genre offers escapism, yet it can also expose the very anxieties it seems to ignore.

nuance.analogy: Escapism is like a warm blanket you pull over your head when the world is too loud; it comforts you, but it doesn't change the room.
nuance.etymology: From 'escape' with the noun suffix '-ism'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as 'ess-KAYP', with the stress on the first syllable.
Confusing 'escapism' with 'escape' as a single event; escapism is a habit or tendency.

senses.definition: Pertaining to eschatology.

core.definition: Relating to eschatology, the theological study of the last things, such as death, judgment, and the end of history.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on 'lah', with a lighter stress on the first syllable. Many learners stress 'ES' too strongly or forget the 'j' sound in the middle.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, used in theology and religious studies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in seminaries, theology classes, sermons on the end times, and academic writing. In casual speech people say 'about the end times' or 'about the afterlife' instead. It is a precise term, so using it in a general conversation may sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Apocalyptic refers to catastrophe or revelation, often dramatic, while eschatological refers more broadly to doctrines about final things.
Millenarian refers specifically to beliefs about a thousand-year reign, while eschatological covers the whole range of end-time doctrine.

examples.everyday: My pastor's sermon was really eschatological, all about what heaven will be like.
examples.professional: Our Bible study group wants to discuss the eschatological themes in Revelation.
examples.analytical: Paul's letters present an eschatological framework in which resurrection and judgment are central.

nuance.analogy: If history is a story, eschatological thinking is the study of its final chapter.
nuance.etymology: From Greek 'eschatos', last, plus '-logy' and '-ical'.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'ES' too strongly and reducing the middle syllables.
Pronouncing the 'ch' as 'sh'; the 'ch' is a hard 'k' sound.

senses.definition: A concentrated coffee beverage brewed by forcing hot water under high pressure through finely ground coffee.
A drink that includes espresso as an ingredient.

core.definition: A small, strong coffee made by forcing hot water under high pressure through finely ground coffee.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable, SPREH, not the first. The first syllable is a short eh, and the ss is a single clear s sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a product, though ordering it can signal that you know coffee well.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say espresso for the strong shot itself and often order it at cafes like Starbucks or local coffee shops. You can say a shot of espresso or ask for a double shot. If you want it diluted, ask for an Americano; for milk, ask for a latte or cappuccino.

distinctions.note: Drip coffee is made by gravity dripping water through grounds and is weaker and larger in volume. Espresso is small and concentrated.
An Americano is espresso diluted with hot water, so it is less intense than a straight espresso shot.

examples.everyday: Can I get a double espresso to go, please?
examples.professional: Let's grab an espresso before the 9 a.m. stand-up so we're awake for the demo.
examples.analytical: The espresso extraction process depends on pressure, grind size, and water temperature, which together determine the crema and flavor.

nuance.analogy: Espresso is like a concentrated essence of coffee, with the same flavor packed into a tiny amount of liquid.
nuance.etymology: From Italian espresso, meaning 'pressed out' or 'expressed', from esprimere.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in ES-presso.
Pronouncing the second vowel as ee, as in ess-PREE-so.
Saying expresso, which is a common spelling and pronunciation error.

espresso.etymology: Italian *espresso*, from *caffè espresso* (“pressed-out coffee”), form of *esprimere* (“to press out”), from Latin *exprimere*, from *ex-* (“out”) + *primere* (“to press”).

conversation.text: I'll have a double espresso, please.
The espresso here is really strong.
After dinner, he always orders an espresso.

senses.definition: Flatness, smoothness; the quality of being flat or level.
The quality of being even (of numbers).

core.definition: The quality of being flat, smooth, or level, or of being equal in amount or balance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on EE. The final syllables are reduced to 'uhn-uhs,' so the -ness is a soft 'nuhs' sound, not a full 'ness.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical or mathematical quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evenness for surfaces and numbers, such as the evenness of paint or the evenness of a sample. In everyday talk people more often say flat, smooth, or level. In statistics and data science, evenness can describe how equally values are distributed across groups.

distinctions.note: Smoothness refers to the absence of bumps, while evenness refers to consistency across a surface or distribution.
Equality is about equal status or treatment, while evenness is about a level or balanced quality.

examples.everyday: I like the evenness of this new paint, because it covers the wall without any streaks.
examples.professional: We measured the evenness of the sample distribution before running the regression.
examples.analytical: The evenness of the data suggests that the sampling method was not biased toward any group.

nuance.analogy: Like a freshly poured layer of concrete that settles flat, evenness describes a surface or distribution with no bumps.
nuance.etymology: From even plus the suffix -ness, forming a noun of quality.
common_mistakes: Confusing evenness with equality; evenness describes balance or level quality, not fair treatment of people.
Pronouncing the ending as a full 'ness' instead of a reduced 'nuhs.'

senses.definition: A programming construct that waits for and dispatches events or messages.

core.definition: A program mechanism that waits for events or messages and runs the matching handler code for each one.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on VENT, and loop rhymes with 'hoop.' Do not stress loop more strongly than event in this compound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a standard term in software development.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use event loop in programming, especially in JavaScript, Node.js, Python asyncio, and GUI frameworks. Developers say things like 'the event loop is blocked' when code runs too long. Outside software, the phrase is not used.

distinctions.note: A general loop repeats code until a condition is met, while an event loop repeatedly waits for and dispatches events.
A thread is a separate path of execution, while an event loop is a single mechanism that handles many events, often on one thread.

examples.everyday: Our coworker says the app freezes because the event loop is busy with one slow task.
examples.professional: We should move the heavy computation off the event loop so the server can keep responding to requests.
examples.analytical: The event loop model explains why a single long-running callback can delay every other task in the system.

nuance.analogy: Like a receptionist who answers each incoming call in turn and sends it to the right person, the event loop takes each event and dispatches it to the right handler.
common_mistakes: Stressing loop as strongly as event, which makes the compound sound unnatural.
Confusing an event loop with a simple for loop; an event loop waits for events rather than counting through a fixed range.

senses.definition: To cry out suddenly, from some strong emotion.
To say suddenly and with strong emotion.

core.definition: To cry out suddenly, or to say something loudly, because of a strong emotion such as surprise, joy, or fear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -SKLAYM. The initial sound is a reduced 'ik,' and the -sk- cluster is pronounced cleanly without a vowel between s and k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a loud, emotional outburst, often one of surprise or joy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exclaim mostly in writing and storytelling: 'She exclaimed, "Look at that!"' In casual speech people more often say yell, shout, or say. A natural reply to an exclamation is to ask what happened or to say 'What? Tell me.'

distinctions.note: Shout describes a loud voice without necessarily showing emotion, while exclaim emphasizes a sudden, emotional outcry.
Say is neutral and general; exclaim adds strong feeling and loudness.

examples.everyday: When I opened the door, my roommate exclaimed, 'You finally fixed the sink!' and I could hear the relief in her voice.
examples.professional: During the review, the manager exclaimed that the new dashboard finally showed the right numbers.
examples.analytical: The narrator exclaims at the moment of revelation, and that outburst marks the turning point of the whole argument.

nuance.analogy: To exclaim is like a kettle whistling suddenly: the feeling builds up and then bursts out loud and fast.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exclamare, 'to cry out,' from ex- 'out' and clamare 'to shout.'
common_mistakes: Using exclaim for everyday talking; it sounds dramatic in casual speech.
Putting the exclamation in quotes without a comma: 'She exclaimed, "Look!"' is the standard form.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word behind exclaim in Luke is anaphōneō (ἀναφωνέω), 'to cry out loudly.' In Luke 1:42, Elizabeth cries out with a loud voice when Mary greets her, showing the joy of the Spirit at the meeting of the two mothers. In Mark 6:49, the disciples cry out in fear when they see Jesus walking on the sea, mistaking him for a ghost.

exclaim.etymology: From Middle French *exclamer*, from Latin *exclamo* (“call out”), from *ex-* + *clāmō* (“to call”).

senses.definition: The act or practice of exhorting.
Language intended to give advice or to urge or encourage.

core.definition: A strong, earnest speech or piece of writing that urges someone to do something, often of a moral or motivational kind.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -tay-, and the final -tion is pronounced 'shun'. Keep the 'or' vowel clear and do not reduce the r in 'exhort'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It implies sincere, serious encouragement, often with a moral or spiritual tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use exhortation in sermons, speeches, commencement addresses and formal writing. In normal conversation people say 'a pep talk' or 'a call to action'. A casual 'pep talk' is far more common for sports or work motivation, and exhortation sounds more solemn.

distinctions.note: A pep talk is informal and short, typically before a game or task, while an exhortation is more serious and formal.
A sermon is a formal religious talk on a text, while an exhortation may be any earnest urging, religious or secular.

examples.everyday: After the game, my coach gave us a short exhortation to keep our heads up.
examples.professional: The vice president's closing exhortation asked every manager to own their metrics.
examples.analytical: Paul's exhortation in Romans 12 moves from doctrine to practice, linking belief with concrete Christian conduct.

nuance.analogy: An exhortation is a verbal push on the back: it aims to move you forward, not just to inform you.
nuance.etymology: From Latin exhortatio, from exhortari 'to urge strongly'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'exhortation to do' instead of 'exhortation to action' or 'an exhortation to do something'.
Pronouncing the middle as 'hor-TAY' with weak stress, which makes the word sound unclear.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek paraklēsis, from parakaleō, means 'calling alongside' and can mean exhortation, encouragement or comfort. Acts 2:40 records Peter exhorting the crowd, Hebrews 13:22 calls the letter a word of exhortation, and Romans 12:8 names exhortation as a gift. These texts present exhortation as earnest, pastoral speech aimed at building up the church.

exhortation.etymology: From Middle English *exhortacioun*, from Old French *exhortacion*, from Latin *exhortātiōnem*, accusative singular of *exhortātiō* (“encouraging; exhortation”), from *exhortor* (“to encourage, exhort”), from *ex* (“out of, from”) + *hortor* (“encourage”).

senses.definition: The doctrine that all events are subject to fate or inevitable necessity, or determined in advance in such a way that human beings cannot alter them.

core.definition: The belief that events are predetermined and cannot be changed, so people should accept whatever happens.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FAY, the first syllable. The middle syllables are reduced, so say the second as tuh and the final as um, not with full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Often negative, suggesting passivity or resignation; in philosophical contexts it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fatalism in discussions of philosophy, religion, politics, and psychology, and sometimes in everyday talk about pessimism. Saying someone has a 'fatalistic attitude' is a mild criticism that they give up too easily. In casual speech, people more often say 'it's just fate' or 'whatever will be will be.'

distinctions.note: Determinism is the broader philosophical view that all events have causes; fatalism adds that outcomes are inevitable regardless of action.
Pessimism is an expectation of bad outcomes; fatalism is the belief that outcomes cannot be changed by effort.

collocations: fatalism in the face of disease

examples.everyday: My uncle has a real fatalism about his health; he says if it's his time, it's his time.
examples.professional: Our team's fatalism about the legacy code made people stop proposing improvements altogether.
examples.analytical: Stoic fatalism and Calvinist predestination both raise the question of whether human choice has any real effect on outcomes.

nuance.analogy: Like a train whose tracks are already laid, so the passenger can watch the scenery but never choose the route.
nuance.etymology: From fatal (from Latin fatum, fate) plus -ism; the suffix denotes a doctrine or belief system.
common_mistakes: Confusing fatalism with fatalistic as the noun; fatalism is the belief, fatalistic is the adjective.
Mispronouncing the stress as fa-TAL-iz-um.

senses.definition: Wild; untamed.
senses.example: In this region, the wild boars can be dangerous, but (perhaps counterintuitively) the feral hogs can be even worse.

senses.definition: Of an animal, wild but descended from domestic or captive ancestors; thus, in the wild, although not necessarily of the wild type.
senses.example: In this region, the wild boars can be dangerous, but (perhaps counterintuitively) the feral hogs can be even worse.

senses.definition: Having the characteristics of an animal; animal-like.
Of a person, contemptible; unruly; misbehaved.
Behaving in an out-of-control way due to enthrallment with a certain thought, behavior, person, etc.
That is a feral character; zoomorphic.
Deadly, fatal.
Of or pertaining to the dead, funereal.
A domesticated (non-human) animal that has returned to the wild; an animal, particularly a domesticated animal, living independently of humans.
A furry character in art or literature which has the appearance of a regular animal (typically quadrupedal), that may or may not be able to communicate with humans or "anthros".
senses.example: The story is about a group of ferals which have to explore the ruins of society after the humans die out.

core.definition: Of an animal, wild after living with people, or having fallen back into a wild state, such as a feral cat.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the r is pronounced clearly, as in American English. Avoid turning the final syllable into 'ee-ul'; it ends with a soft, reduced schwa-l.

nuance.connotation: neutral to slightly negative. It suggests wildness, disorder or danger, and it is used for animals and sometimes for people behaving in a wild way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'feral' for cats, dogs, hogs and other animals that were once domestic and now live wild, especially in cities or on farms. Used about people, it is strong and can sound insulting or dramatic, as in 'feral teenagers.' In everyday talk you might hear 'feral cat colony' at a shelter or a neighbor's comment about strays.

distinctions.note: Wild is the general word for not tamed; feral specifically means an animal that was domestic and returned to the wild.
A stray is usually a domestic animal that is lost or homeless and may still depend on people, while a feral animal has no contact with humans.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor feeds the feral cats behind the garage every evening.
examples.professional: The county animal services office tracks feral cat populations to plan its spay and neuter program.
examples.analytical: The author describes the protagonist's feral behavior as a loss of the social restraints that once shaped him.

nuance.analogy: A feral animal is like a houseplant that escapes into the woods and grows wild again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin fera, 'wild beast'.
common_mistakes: Using 'feral' as a synonym for any wild animal, when it specifically refers to formerly domestic animals.
Pronouncing the word with two syllables, as in 'FEER-ul'.

senses.definition: Obvious and offensive; blatant; scandalous.
senses.example: a flagrant, unforgivably outrageous disregard for human life

core.definition: Obvious and shocking, especially a wrong or violation done openly without any attempt to hide it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FLAY. The final syllable is a weak schwa, and the r should be clear, not dropped.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; it stresses that something bad is obvious and unashamed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'flagrant' often in news, sports, and workplace talk, for example 'a flagrant foul' or 'a flagrant violation'. In casual speech people may say 'blatant' or 'totally obvious'. It is strong, so use it when you mean the wrongdoing is clearly unacceptable.

distinctions.note: 'Blatant' is common in everyday speech and stresses obviousness; 'flagrant' adds a stronger sense of outrageous offense.
'Obvious' is neutral and can be harmless; 'flagrant' always describes something bad.

examples.everyday: That driver cut right in front of us, which was a flagrant move.
examples.professional: The manager's flagrant disregard for the safety rules led to the audit.
examples.analytical: The author treats the regime's flagrant hypocrisy as the central evidence of its moral collapse.

nuance.analogy: A red flag waved in plain view, impossible to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Latin flagrans, 'burning,' from flagrare, 'to burn.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as 'fla-GRANT' with stress on the second syllable.
Using it for mild errors; it means serious and obvious, so it sounds too strong for small mistakes.

flagrant.etymology: From Middle French *flagrant*, from Latin *flagrantem*, present participle of *flagrare* (“blaze, burn”).

senses.definition: A van (or wagon) that serves as a restaurant kitchen to sell hot food to customers.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see food,‎ truck.
A food delivery truck.

core.definition: A large vehicle with a built-in kitchen that sells prepared food to customers on the street or at events.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TRUCK, and the American r is clear and retroflex. The vowel in 'truck' is short and relaxed, not 'trook.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and casual, often associated with creative, affordable meals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'food truck' for a mobile restaurant that parks at offices, festivals, and street corners. People often say 'There's a great food truck near the park on Thursdays.' The word 'truck' here means a large vehicle, not a pickup. Some cities call them 'street food' or 'mobile kitchens' in formal rules.

distinctions.note: A food cart is usually pushed or towed and smaller, while a food truck is a motorized vehicle with a full kitchen.
A restaurant has a fixed building, while a food truck moves between locations.

examples.everyday: Let's grab lunch from that food truck by the library; their tacos are amazing.
examples.professional: The company hired a food truck for the team offsite, so nobody had to leave the campus.
examples.analytical: The rise of food trucks shows how small-scale food businesses can use mobility to avoid high rent in dense cities.

nuance.analogy: Like a restaurant kitchen on wheels, a food truck brings the meal to where people already gather.
nuance.etymology: 'Food' from Old English 'foda'; 'truck' from Latin 'trochus' (wheel) through French 'troque'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'food car' instead of 'food truck' in American English.
Mispronouncing 'truck' with a long oo vowel.

conversation.text: There's a taco food truck parked outside our office every Tuesday.
Let's hit the food trucks at the festival for lunch.
My friend quit her job to open a food truck.

senses.definition: A natural source of water; a spring.
An artificial, usually ornamental, water feature (usually in a garden or public place) consisting of one or more streams of water originating from a statue or other structure.
senses.example: His house is right beside that fountain on Street 15.

senses.definition: The structure from which an artificial fountain can issue.
A reservoir from which liquid can be drawn.
A source or origin of a flow (e.g. of favors or knowledge).
A roundel barry wavy argent and azure.
A juggling pattern typically done with an even number of props where each prop is caught by the same hand that throws it.
A soda fountain.
A drink poured from a soda fountain, or the cup it is poured into.
A ground-based firework that projects sparks similar to a water fountain.
Anything that resembles a fountain in operation.
To flow or gush as if from a fountain.
senses.example: Lava fountained from the volcano.

core.definition: A decorative structure in a garden or public place that shoots water into the air or a basin.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, FOWN. The final syllable is a reduced tun, with the t often flapped or softened to a light d between vowels in casual speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; fountains suggest beauty, refreshment, and public places.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fountain for ornamental water features in parks, malls, and plazas, and for drinking fountains, which are common in schools and public buildings. In restaurants, a soda fountain can refer to a drink dispenser. Biblically and poetically, fountain can mean a source of life or water.

distinctions.note: A spring is a natural source of water coming from the ground; a fountain is usually artificial or ornamental.
Water fountain in American English usually means a drinking fountain in a public building; fountain alone more often means an ornamental water feature.

examples.everyday: Let's meet by the fountain in the park after lunch.
examples.professional: The fountain in the lobby was shut off for maintenance, so we took the stairs.
examples.analytical: Scripture repeatedly pictures God as a fountain of life, the source from which all life flows.

nuance.analogy: Like a faucet that never runs out, bubbling up from its own source.
nuance.etymology: From Old French fontaine, from Latin fontana, from fons, 'spring'.
common_mistakes: Confusing fountain with the natural word spring
Saying water fountain for a park fountain (Americans usually mean a drinking fountain)
Stressing the second syllable
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, a fountain usually means a spring or source of water, and it is a central image for God as the source of life. The Hebrew word maqor means spring or source, and the Greek word pege means spring or fountain. Psalm 36:9 says that with God is the fountain of life. Jeremiah 2:13 calls God the fountain of living waters that the people forsook for broken cisterns. Revelation 21:6 speaks of giving water from the spring of the water of life.

fountain.etymology: From Middle English; from Old French *fontaine* (whence modern *fontaine*); from Late Latin *fontana*, from Latin *fontanus*, *fontaneus*, adjectives from *fons* (“source, spring”).

senses.definition: The loose collection of fictional works pertaining to a particular fictional universe, including literary, film, or television series from various sources, generally when all authorized by a copyright holder or similar authority.
senses.example: the Star Wars franchise

senses.definition: The collection of organizations in the history of a sports team; the tradition of a sports team as an entity, extending beyond the contemporary organization.
senses.example: The Whalers' home city of Hartford was one of many for the franchise.

senses.definition: A business operating under such authorization, a franchisee.
The right to vote at a public election or referendum; see: suffrage.
A right or privilege officially granted to a person, a group of people, or a company by a government.
An acknowledgment of a corporation's existence and ownership.
The authorization granted by a company to sell or distribute its goods or services in a certain area.
senses.example: McDonald’s has exported its franchise.

senses.definition: A legal exemption from jurisdiction.
The membership of a corporation or state; citizenship.
The district or jurisdiction to which a particular privilege extends; the limits of an immunity; hence, an asylum or sanctuary.
The positive influence on the buying behavior of customers exerted by the reputation of a company or a brand.
Exemption from constraint or oppression; freedom; liberty.
To confer certain powers on; grant a franchise to; authorize.
To give to others the rights to sell or distribute (goods or services).
To set free; invest with a franchise or privilege; enfranchise.

core.definition: A business licensed by a larger company to sell its products or services under the company's name, usually in a local outlet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, FRAN-chise, and keep the ch sound soft. The final s is pronounced z, and learners often say fran-KHEEZ or fran-CHISE with the wrong stress.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a franchise is a normal, respectable way to run a small business, though a chain can feel impersonal to some customers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use franchise mostly for a local restaurant, gym, or store that belongs to a national brand, such as a McDonald's or a Planet Fitness. People say they are thinking of buying a franchise or that a store is a franchise, meaning the owner pays fees to use the brand. In sports and entertainment, the same word also means a team or a series of movies, which is a separate sense.

distinctions.note: A chain is a group of outlets under one name, which may be owned directly by the company; a franchise is a single outlet owned by a separate person under license.
A branch is run directly by the parent company, while a franchise is independently owned and operated under a franchise agreement.

examples.everyday: My cousin bought a Subway franchise near the highway, so she works like crazy but she is her own boss.
examples.professional: Our legal team reviewed the franchise agreement before we signed the lease for the new location.
examples.analytical: A franchise model distributes financial risk between the brand owner and the local operator, which is why the arrangement persists across industries.

nuance.analogy: A franchise is like renting a proven recipe along with the restaurant's name: you do the cooking and the business, but you follow the brand's rules.
nuance.etymology: From Old French franchise, meaning freedom or privilege, from franc, free.
common_mistakes: Saying fran-KHEEZ with stress on the second syllable.
Confusing franchise (the business) with franchisee (the person who owns it), as in saying I am a franchise when you mean you own one.

franchise.etymology: From Middle English *franchise*, *fraunchise*, from Old French *franchise* (“freedom”), a derivative of *franc* (“free”).

conversation.text: That franchise has like ten movies now.
The Star Wars franchise is huge.
He's the best player in franchise history.

senses.definition: An advocate of frequentism.
Of or pertaining to frequentism.

core.definition: A statistician who defines probability as the long-run frequency of events in repeated trials.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, FREE. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, and the t sound is clear before the final ist.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It names a school of thought without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frequentist in academic statistics, data science, and research methods. It is often contrasted with Bayesian in classes and papers. It is a precise term, so people use it when discussing methods, not in everyday conversation.

distinctions.note: A Bayesian treats probability as a degree of belief updated with data, while a frequentist treats it as long-run frequency in repeated trials.
Frequentism is the philosophy or method itself, while frequentist names a person or describes something related to it.

examples.everyday: My roommate who studies math says she is a frequentist, so she does not like the way I talk about gut feelings.
examples.professional: Our analysis team uses a frequentist approach, so we report p-values and confidence intervals for each test.
examples.analytical: A frequentist interprets a confidence interval as a procedure that captures the true parameter in a stated proportion of repeated samples.

nuance.analogy: A frequentist is like a coin-flipper who trusts the long run: flip enough times and the proportion of heads settles where it should.
nuance.etymology: From frequent, from Latin frequens, crowded or repeated, plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Using frequentist as a general word for someone who is frequently present; it is a technical statistics term.
Confusing frequentist with frequency distribution, which is a table or graph.

senses.definition: A cover of minute ice crystals on objects that are exposed to the air. Frost is formed by the same process as dew, except that the temperature of the frosted object is below freezing.
The cold weather that causes these ice crystals to form.
Coldness or insensibility; severity or rigidity of character.
A shade of white, like that of frost.
senses.example: frost:

senses.definition: A kind of light diffuser.
A disappointment; a cheat.
To cover with frost.
To become covered with frost.
To coat (something, e.g. a cake) with icing to resemble frost.
To anger or annoy.
senses.example: I think the boss's decision frosted him a bit.

senses.definition: To sharpen (the points of a horse's shoe) to prevent it from slipping on ice.
To bleach individual strands of hair while leaving adjacent strands untouched.

core.definition: A thin layer of tiny ice crystals that forms on cold surfaces when the air temperature falls below freezing, or the cold weather that causes it.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the open 'aw' of cot-caught speakers in many areas, so say it like 'frawst'. Don't add an extra vowel before the st cluster. The r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: neutral in weather talk; can be poetic or suggest coldness and harshness in literature.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use frost for the white crystals on windows and grass on winter mornings, and they say 'frost warning' or 'hard frost' in weather reports. Gardeners watch the frost date closely. Figurative uses such as 'a frost in her manner' sound literary.

distinctions.note: Ice is solid water in general, while frost is a delicate layer of crystals formed from water vapor on cold surfaces.
Freeze means water turns solid at or below 32°F; frost is the crystal layer that can form without a full freeze.

examples.everyday: Scrape the frost off the windshield before you drive to work.
examples.professional: The farm sent an alert about a hard frost tonight, so the crew will cover the young plants.
examples.analytical: In the poem the frost is a symbol of a cold, unfeeling world that quietly covers everything.

nuance.analogy: Frost is like the thin white sugar dusting on a cold donut, forming gradually on a surface that is colder than the air around it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'forst', related to Old Norse 'frost' and German 'Frost', ultimately from a root meaning to freeze.
common_mistakes: Saying 'frost' with a long 'o', such as 'frohst', instead of the open 'aw' sound.
Confusing frost with 'snow', which is falling precipitation rather than a surface coating.
Using 'frost' as a verb for making ice, when the verb means to cover with frost or icing.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture frost is part of the cold of winter, often named alongside snow and ice as a sign of God's power over creation. The Hebrew word behind it is kerach (ice, frost), which the RSV renders in various ways in the poetry of creation and winter. Psalm 147:16 describes God spreading frost like ashes over the earth, a picture of his command over the seasons. Psalm 148:8 lists frost among the created things that praise the LORD, and Job 38:29 asks who gives birth to the frost of heaven, pointing to God's sovereignty over nature.

frost.etymology: From Middle English *frost*, from an unmetathesized variant of Old English *forst* (“frost”), from Proto-Germanic **frustaz* (“frost”), from Proto-Indo-European **prews-* (“to freeze; frost”).

senses.definition: A hilly region east of the Jordan River in the Bible, known for its good pastureland and for a healing balm.

core.definition: A hilly region east of the Jordan River in the Bible, known for its good pastureland and for a healing balm.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GIL. The last two syllables are reduced to a light uh-d, so say GIL-ee-ud, not gil-EE-ahd.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In religious settings it carries a tone of comfort and healing because of the balm passage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet Gilead in Bible study, sermons, and the novel The Handmaid's Tale, where it is a fictional state. In church talk, people often say there is a balm in Gilead, a phrase from a famous spiritual that refers to healing and hope.

distinctions.note: Gilead the place is the Transjordan highland; Gilead in The Handmaid's Tale is a fictional state, not a real place.

examples.everyday: Our Bible study group is reading about Jacob and Laban, and everyone keeps mentioning Gilead.
examples.professional: In my seminar paper, I compare Gilead's role in Israel's tribal history with the settlement of Transjordan.
examples.analytical: Jeremiah's question about whether there is no balm in Gilead assumes the region's fame for healing, which makes his despair sharper.

nuance.analogy: Gilead works like a famous landmark in a story: its name carries meaning far beyond its map location.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew place name; the meaning is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, saying gil-EE-ad
Confusing the Bible region with the fictional state in The Handmaid's Tale
nuance.biblical_note: Gilead is a mountainous region east of the Jordan, in the territory of tribes such as Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh. Genesis 31:47-48 links the name to Jacob and Laban's covenant heap. Jeremiah 8:22 refers to the balm of Gilead, a medicinal resin, to express the absence of healing for Judah. Judges 11:1 identifies Jephthah the Gileadite as a leader from this region.

senses.definition: Exuberantly or triumphantly joyful.

core.definition: Showing open, delighted joy, often about something good or about someone else's trouble.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is a reduced 'fuhl', with the vowel almost silent. Do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: positive for pure delight, but negative when the joy is at someone's misfortune.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gleeful for children, kids on holidays, or people celebrating a win. When the joy is at someone else's expense, the word can sound mocking. It describes a person's expression or mood, so you can say 'a gleeful grin'.

distinctions.note: Happy is the general, neutral word for pleasure. Gleeful is stronger and more visible, with noisy or playful energy.
Elated is more formal and suggests high spirits after a success. Gleeful is livelier and often childlike.

examples.everyday: The kids were gleeful when they heard school was canceled because of the snow.
examples.professional: The sales team was gleeful after closing the biggest deal of the quarter.
examples.analytical: Her gleeful tone in the essay signals satire rather than sincere praise, which changes how the reader should judge the argument.

nuance.analogy: Like a kid on the last day of school, running out the door with nothing to hold back the joy.
nuance.etymology: From glee (from Old English gleo, meaning entertainment or mirth) plus the suffix -ful.
common_mistakes: Using gleeful for quiet or calm happiness. The word implies open, energetic delight.
Mispronouncing it with a long 'a' in the second syllable. It is GLEE-fuhl.

senses.definition: To look at carefully; to scrutinize; to analyze.
senses.example: Please go over the reports to make sure we haven't missed anything.

senses.definition: To turn out successful; to be well-received.
senses.example: That song really went over with the audience.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see go,‎ over.
senses.example: I'm going over to my friend's house because I've already gone over my weekly quota.

senses.definition: To create a response or impression.
senses.example: Playing a radio in the office did not go over well with his coworkers.

senses.definition: To spray paint graffiti over someone else's graffiti.
To encompass or cover (a subject).
senses.example: In first period, we're going over the basics of cell biology.

senses.definition: To score a try.
To convert or switch sides.
senses.example: He went over to the finance department's side in this dispute.

senses.definition: To convert to Roman Catholicism.

core.definition: To review or examine something carefully, especially to check it, explain it, or find mistakes.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable of over, OH, and the final -er is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so say OH-vur, not OH-ver. Linking the two words gives a smooth goh-OH-vur sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical word for careful review, and it is positive when the goal is to catch errors or prepare.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, 'go over' is a common way to ask for a review, as in 'Can we go over the budget before the call?' It is less formal than 'review' and 'examine', which suit written reports. It can also mean to be well-received, but in everyday talk the review sense is most useful. A natural reply is 'Sure, I'll send the file first.'

distinctions.note: Review is a more formal word for examining something in detail, often in writing or a formal process, while go over is more conversational.
Go through often means checking each item in a list or sequence, while go over focuses on understanding or reviewing the whole.

examples.everyday: Can we go over the directions one more time before we leave?
examples.professional: Let's go over the dashboard numbers in the meeting before we send them to finance.
examples.analytical: The argument must go over each premise carefully, since a single weak step undermines the whole conclusion.

nuance.analogy: Like running your eyes slowly over a map before a trip, checking each route.
common_mistakes: Using 'go over' with 'to' as in 'go over to the report' when you mean review it; say 'go over the report'.
Confusing the review sense with the success sense ('the idea went over well' means it was well-received).

conversation.text: Let's go over the plan one more time before the meeting.
Can you go over my resume and give me some feedback?
How did your presentation go over with the client?
We went over our budget on the trip.
Let's go over the agenda before the client joins.
Can we go over the budget one more time?
Sorry, we're going to go over by a few minutes.

senses.definition: An ancient region in northern Mesopotamia, along the Habor River, where the Assyrians settled captive Israelites.

core.definition: An ancient region in northern Mesopotamia, along the Habor River, where the Assyrians settled captive Israelites.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable has a short a as in ran.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a historical and biblical place name.
nuance.usage_note: Gozan appears mainly in Bible study, ancient history, and archaeology. Americans usually mention the Assyrian context when they name it. It is rarely used in everyday conversation.

examples.everyday: We read about Gozan in 2 Kings, where the Assyrians sent captured Israelites to that region.
examples.professional: In the lecture, the archaeologist showed how Gozan connected to Assyrian trade and military routes.
examples.analytical: Scholars debate whether the Israelites exiled to Gozan were eventually absorbed into surrounding peoples.

common_mistakes: Pronouncing it GO-zahn or GOZ-un; the stress belongs on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: Gozan was a region in northern Mesopotamia on the Habor River, under Assyrian control. In 2 Kings 17:6 the king of Assyria settles captured Israelites in Halah and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes. 1 Chronicles 5:26 lists Gozan among the places to which the Reubenites, Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh were carried into exile.

senses.definition: A tract of land in which the dead are buried.
A final storage place for collections of things that are no longer useful or useable.
The discard pile, in some trading card games.
A period very early in the morning in which there is very little activity.
senses.example: graveyard shift, graveyard slot, graveyard watch

senses.definition: Synonym of suicide (“a beverage combining all available flavors at a soda fountain”).
A team where players are sent when they are not useful, or a team where players become useless if sent there.

core.definition: An area of land where dead people are buried; a cemetery, especially a small or old one next to a church.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the first syllable, GRAYV, and the second syllable is a lighter yard with a clear r. Do not stress both parts equally or say GRAVE-yard with a weak second part.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly somber. It can be used literally or metaphorically, which may sound dark or humorous.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use graveyard for a small or older burial ground, especially near a church, while cemetery is the general and more formal word. The word is also used in phrases like graveyard shift, and in a metaphorical sense for a place where ideas or projects die.

distinctions.note: Cemetery is the general and formal term used in public records and most modern places. Graveyard is more informal and often suggests a smaller churchyard setting.
Churchyard specifically means the land around a church used for burials, while graveyard can refer to any burial ground.

examples.everyday: We walked through the old graveyard behind the church on Sunday afternoon.
examples.professional: The company's old software became a graveyard of unused features that nobody maintains.
examples.analytical: Ezekiel's vision of the valley of dry bones uses the image of graves and a graveyard to show God's power to restore life.

nuance.analogy: A graveyard for ideas is like a drawer where old sketches go to be forgotten.
nuance.etymology: From grave and yard, combining the Old English graef, a burial place, with the word for an enclosed area.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural in American speech.
Using graveyard for a cemetery in a formal or legal document, where cemetery is the usual word.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word qever means grave or tomb. Ezekiel 37:12-13 (RSV) describes God opening the graves of his people and bringing them up from them. Matthew 27:52-53 (RSV) reports that tombs were opened and holy people raised after Christ's death.

senses.definition: In a grievous manner, severely.

core.definition: In a way that causes great pain, harm or sorrow; severely, as in grievously injured or grievously wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, reduce the middle syllable, and end with a clear ly. Do not add extra syllables between the v and the s.

nuance.connotation: Negative and strong; it signals severe harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use grievously almost only in formal writing, news reports and legal contexts, as in grievously injured. In casual speech they say badly or seriously. It pairs with words like wounded, injured, mistaken or wronged.

distinctions.note: Badly is everyday and general, while grievously is formal and stresses severe harm or sorrow.
Seriously is common and neutral, while grievously is stronger and more dramatic.

examples.everyday: My cousin was grievously hurt in a fall, but she's home now.
examples.professional: The bug grievously affected our billing system, so we rolled back the release.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the nation was grievously wronged by its own leaders.

nuance.analogy: If bad is a bruise, grievously is a deep wound that takes a long time to heal.
nuance.etymology: From grievous plus -ly, from Old French grevos, from Latin gravis, heavy.
common_mistakes: Using grievously in casual speech, where badly or seriously sounds more natural.
Dropping the middle syllable, saying GREE-slee instead of GREE-vus-lee.

senses.definition: A cat, especially an elderly female.

core.definition: An old female cat; a cat, especially an elderly female, often used with affection or mock disdain.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MAL, and the final syllable is a reduced unstressed vowel, not a long "een." Many learners stress the first syllable instead.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly humorous; it can sound playful or slightly condescending toward an old woman, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in daily speech. You will meet it in older novels, poetry, or witty writing, where it is a colorful way to say "cat." Saying it about an actual pet in casual conversation would sound like a deliberate joke.

distinctions.note: "Cat" is the ordinary word; "grimalkin" is literary, old-fashioned and often playful.
A tabby is a cat with a striped or blotched coat, which describes appearance, while grimalkin describes an old female cat.

collocations: a grimalkin dozing by the fire

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's old grimalkin sleeps on her porch every afternoon.
examples.professional: The marketing copy for the vintage pet food brand used the word grimalkin to sound charmingly old-fashioned.
examples.analytical: Shakespeare's witches are sometimes read through the figure of the grimalkin, a familiar animal that carried the suspicion of witchcraft.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a cat "Her Majesty" in a joke: it is a formal-sounding title for a plain animal.
nuance.etymology: From "Grey" (gray) plus "Malkin," an old name for a cat, probably from the name Maud or Matilda.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (GRIM-al-kin) instead of the second.
Using it as a neutral everyday word for any cat in casual speech.

senses.definition: The mathematical theory of groups.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see group,‎ theory; a theory about (particular kinds of) groups.

core.definition: The branch of mathematics that studies groups, which are sets with an operation that is associative, has an identity, and has inverses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress theory on the first syllable of the word, THEE, with the ending ree reduced to a light ee. The th is unvoiced, so place your tongue between your teeth.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term in mathematics and physics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use group theory in university mathematics, physics and cryptography. It refers to the abstract study of symmetry and structure, not to social groups. In casual talk, it is rarely used outside technical circles.

distinctions.note: Set theory studies collections of objects in general, while group theory studies sets with a specific algebraic operation.
A group in math is a structured set with an operation, not a collection of people.

examples.everyday: My son is studying group theory, so the homework is way over my head.
examples.professional: Our cryptography team uses group theory to choose secure parameters for the key exchange.
examples.analytical: Group theory reveals how symmetry constrains possible structures, which is why it explains so many physical laws.

nuance.analogy: Like a set of rotations of a square that can be combined, undone and kept in the same family.
nuance.etymology: Group comes from French groupe, from Italian gruppo; theory comes from Greek theōria, a looking at or contemplation.
common_mistakes: Confusing the mathematical group with a social group.
Using the plural groups theory; the phrase is normally singular.

senses.definition: The quality of readily believing information, truthful or otherwise, usually to an absurd extent.

core.definition: A tendency to believe things too easily, even when they are false or unlikely; willingness to be fooled.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, BIL. The first vowel is a short u, as in 'cup', and the final -ity sounds like 'ih-tee' with a reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a weakness, and saying someone has gullibility can sound critical or insulting.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gullibility when talking about scams, advertising, or politics, for example 'the scam works because of people's gullibility.' In everyday talk people often say 'he will believe anything' instead. It is a serious word, so use it with care when speaking about a friend.

distinctions.note: Naivete describes a lack of experience or worldliness and can be affectionate; gullibility describes actually being fooled and is more critical.
Credulity is the more formal and technical word for believing too readily; gullibility is the everyday word.

examples.everyday: I can't believe you fell for that prize email; you have to watch your gullibility online.
examples.professional: Our phishing test showed that even experienced staff can display gullibility when a request appears to come from a manager.
examples.analytical: Gullibility is not simply stupidity; people often trust sources that look authoritative, which scammers deliberately exploit.

nuance.analogy: Gullibility is like a screen door with no latch: anything that knocks gets let in.
nuance.etymology: Derived from 'gullible' by adding the suffix '-ity'; 'gullible' comes from the Middle English-era verb 'gull', meaning to dupe.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the middle as 'guh-LIB-ih-lih-tee'; the stress is on BIL.
Confusing it with 'gullibleness', which is less common in American writing.

senses.definition: A writer of any of the Hagiographa․
Someone who writes the biography of a saint.
Someone who writes in an excessively flattering and laudatory way about a person (as if that person were a saint).

core.definition: A person who writes the lives of saints, or one who writes about someone in an overly flattering way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, AH. The g's are hard, as in 'go'. The ending -pher is a reduced 'fur', and the a in the stressed syllable is 'ah'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for a writer of saints' lives; negative when it implies uncritical, worshipful writing.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American writing the word is mostly used critically, as when a reviewer says a biographer is a hagiographer of a politician or CEO. In religious scholarship it is neutral. It is an educated word, rare in speech.

distinctions.note: A biographer writes about any life, ideally with balance; a hagiographer idealizes.
A sycophant flatters a person for gain; a hagiographer praises in writing, often sincerely.
An apologist defends a belief or person with arguments; a hagiographer celebrates with narrative.

collocations: a hagiographer rather than a historian

examples.everyday: That author is basically a hagiographer; he never mentions a single flaw.
examples.professional: The reviewer called the biographer a hagiographer, noting that the book ignored the founder's controversies.
examples.analytical: The early hagiographer shaped the saint's memory according to the conventions of the genre, not those of modern history.

nuance.analogy: A hagiographer paints with a halo brush: everything comes out glowing.
nuance.etymology: From Greek hagios, 'holy', plus -grapher, 'writer'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable: 'HAG-ee-og-ra-fer'.
Pronouncing the g as j: 'haj-ee'.
Using it as a neutral synonym for 'biographer'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hagiographa are the Writings, the third division of the Hebrew Bible (Ketuvim), including Psalms, Proverbs and Job. The word's older sense is a writer of one of these books.

senses.definition: To move or act in a quick fashion.
To make someone speed up or make something happen quicker.
To cause some scheduled event to happen earlier.

core.definition: To move or act more quickly, or to cause something to happen sooner than expected.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and let the final -en be a syllabic n with no separate vowel, so it sounds like 'HAY-sn.' Non-native speakers often add an extra 'eh' sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can sound a bit formal or literary compared with 'speed up' or 'hurry.'
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people usually say 'speed up,' 'hurry up,' or 'move things along.' Hasten shows up in writing, formal announcements, and speeches, such as 'We hope to hasten the process.' A natural reply to a formal announcement is simply 'That would be great.'

distinctions.note: Speed up is the everyday phrase for going faster, while hasten sounds more formal and often describes making an outcome arrive sooner.
Accelerate is common in technical and business writing about increasing speed or rate, while hasten suggests a more general or literary sense.

examples.everyday: Let's grab a taxi to hasten things along, because the movie starts at seven.
examples.professional: Automating the report generation should hasten our weekly reviews.
examples.analytical: Some theologians argue that human action cannot hasten the coming of the kingdom, which depends on God's own timing.

nuance.analogy: To hasten is like adding fuel to a fire: the flame does not change, but it grows and spreads faster.
nuance.etymology: From haste (noun), formed in Middle English from the noun haste.
common_mistakes: Using 'hasten' with a person as the object in casual speech, as in 'I hastened him,' which sounds stiff.
Pronouncing the final -en as a full syllable instead of a syllabic n.

senses.definition: The part of a shoe's sole which supports the foot's heel.
The rear part of a sock or similar covering for the foot.
The part of the palm of a hand closest to the wrist.
senses.example: He drove the heel of his hand into the man's nose.

senses.definition: A high-heeled shoe.
The back, upper part of the stock.
The last or lowest part of anything.
senses.example: the heel of a mast

senses.definition: The base of a bun sliced in half lengthwise.
A contemptible, unscrupulous, inconsiderate, or thoughtless person.
A headlining wrestler regarded as a "bad guy," whose ring persona embodies villainous or reprehensible traits and demonstrates characteristics of a braggart and a bully.
The cards set aside for later use in a patience or solitaire game.
Anything resembling a human heel in shape; a protuberance; a knob.
The obtuse angle of the lower end of a rafter set sloping.
The short side of an angled cut.
The part of a club head's face nearest the shaft.
The lower end of the bit (cutting edge) of an axehead, as opposed to the toe (upper end).
The part of a carding machine's flat nearest the cylinder.
Material stored in a smelting furnace between batches.
The rear part of the foot, where it joins the leg.
The thickening of the neck of a stringed instrument where it attaches to the body.
The lower end of a timber in a frame, as a post or rafter.
The junction between the keel and the stempost of a vessel; an angular wooden join connecting the two.
The act of inclining or canting from a vertical position; a cant.
To follow at somebody's heels; to chase closely.
senses.example: She called to her dog to heel.

senses.definition: To cause to follow at somebody’s heels (transitive).
To add a heel to, or increase the size of the heel of (a shoe or boot).
To kick with the heel.
senses.example: she heeled her horse forward

senses.definition: To perform by the use of the heels, as in dancing, running, etc.
To arm with a gaff, as a cock for fighting.
To hit (the ball) with the heel of the club.
To make (a fair catch) standing with one foot forward, the heel on the ground and the toe up.
At Yale University, to work as a heeler or student journalist.
To incline to one side; to tilt.

core.definition: As a noun, the rear part of the foot or of a shoe, below the ankle; as a verb, to add a heel to a shoe or to follow closely behind someone.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long ē, rhyming with 'feel' and 'real'. Keep the l clear at the end, which is a dark l in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; the verb 'heel' in a command, as in 'heel!' to a dog, can sound stern.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'heel' most often for the back of a shoe or the back of the foot, as in 'my heel hurts'. In shoe shopping, people talk about 'heel height' and 'low heels'. The verb is less common in everyday speech, except in dog training, where 'heel' means walk closely beside the owner.

distinctions.note: The ankle is the joint above the heel, while the heel is the back part of the foot below it.
The sole is the bottom of the shoe or foot, while the heel is only the back section of that sole.

examples.everyday: My new shoes have high heels, and after an hour my feet really hurt.
examples.professional: The shoe designers want to lower the heel height to improve comfort for workers on their feet all day.
examples.analytical: In Genesis the image of the serpent striking the heel contrasts with the head that is crushed, and interpreters read it as a sign of enduring conflict.

nuance.analogy: The heel is like the foundation stone at the back of a house, which bears the weight as you step.
nuance.etymology: From Old English hēla, meaning 'heel of the foot'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'heel' like 'hill' or 'heal' inconsistently; 'heel' and 'heal' sound the same, so context matters.
Using 'heel' to mean the whole foot instead of only the back part.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the heel is a body part and an image of vulnerability, struggle, and treachery. Genesis 3:15 speaks of the serpent striking the heel of the woman's offspring, while that offspring crushes the serpent's head. Psalm 41:9 describes a close friend who lifts up his heel against the psalmist, a picture of betrayal. The Hebrew word 'āqēb means heel, and it gives the name Jacob, who is said to have grasped his brother's heel at birth in Genesis 25:26.

heel.etymology: From Middle English *hele*, from Old English *hēla*, from **hą̄hilō*, from Proto-Germanic **hanhilaz*, diminutive of Proto-Germanic **hanhaz* (“heel, hock”), equivalent to *hock* + *le*.

senses.definition: A wise man in the Old Testament, traditionally credited with Psalm 88 and named among the sages of Solomon's time.

core.definition: A wise man in the Old Testament, traditionally credited with Psalm 88 and named among the sages of Solomon's time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a long 'ee' vowel. The final syllable is a weak 'uhn' sound, not 'man' with a strong a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a biblical name and carries no everyday connotation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans would mainly encounter 'Heman' in Bible study, sermons, or commentaries. In conversation it is a name for a biblical figure, not a common word. Be aware that 'Heman' is not used as a common English word or as a personal name in everyday American life.

distinctions.note: Ethan is another wise man named in 1 Kings 4:31 alongside Heman, so the two are often mentioned together.

examples.everyday: My Bible study group is reading Psalm 88 this week, and it's attributed to Heman.
examples.professional: In the seminary course, we compared Heman's wisdom with that of Ethan in 1 Kings 4:31.
examples.analytical: The superscription of Psalm 88 names Heman the Ezrahite, and scholars debate whether this attribution refers to the same figure named among Solomon's sages.

nuance.analogy: Heman is like a name in a family tree that appears in several places, each time linked to a different story.
nuance.etymology: Hebrew personal name (Heman), of uncertain meaning.
common_mistakes: Confusing Heman with Haman, the villain of the book of Esther; they are different people.
Pronouncing it with a short a; the first vowel is a long e.
nuance.biblical_note: Heman the Ezrahite is named in 1 Kings 4:31 among the wise men surpassed by Solomon, and he is also named in 1 Chronicles 2:6 as a son of Zerah. Psalm 88 carries his name in its superscription, and it is one of the darkest lament psalms in the Psalter. The Hebrew name is 'Heman', and scholars debate its meaning.

senses.definition: A scholarly approach to the Bible that studies each text's sources, authorship, historical setting, and development over time.

core.definition: A scholarly approach to the Bible that studies each text's sources, authorship, historical setting, and development over time.

pronunciation.tip: Respell each word with its own stress: his-TOR-ih-kul, KRIT-ih-kul, METH-ud. The 'th' in 'method' is voiceless, and the final syllable is reduced to 'ud.' Note the flap-like 'ih' in 'KRIT-ih-kul.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in scholarship; positive for those valuing rigor, and negative for some conservatives who see it as undermining faith.
nuance.usage_note: Common in seminaries and biblical studies programs. It includes source, form, redaction, and textual criticism. 'Critical' here means careful analysis, not fault-finding.

distinctions.note: Higher criticism is an older name for the study of authorship, date, and sources, which is central to the historical-critical method.
Lower, or textual, criticism reconstructs the original wording from manuscripts, while the historical-critical method asks about origins and context.
The grammatical-historical method seeks the author's intended meaning in context, usually without the source and redaction theories of the historical-critical method.

examples.everyday: My professor said the historical-critical method asks who wrote the text, when, and why.
examples.professional: The commentary uses the historical-critical method alongside literary and theological analysis.
examples.analytical: While the historical-critical method clarified the Bible's human settings, it has been criticized for sometimes treating the texts as only historical artifacts.

nuance.analogy: It treats the Bible like an archaeological dig, studying each layer and where it came from.
nuance.etymology: Historical from Greek historia 'inquiry'; critical from Greek kritikos 'able to judge'; method from Greek methodos 'pursuit, way.'
common_mistakes: Thinking 'critical' means hostile to the Bible.
Misplacing stress, as in 'HIS-tor-i-cal.'
Treating it as identical to a purely literal reading.

traditions.view: Embraced officially since Divino Afflante Spiritu (1943) and Dei Verbum as a valuable tool, to be used within the Church's faith and Tradition.
Orthodox scholars use its findings selectively, but generally insist that Scripture be read within the Church's Tradition and patristic interpretation, not by method alone.
Widely used in mainline Protestant scholarship; many evangelicals accept parts of it, such as textual and historical study, while rejecting its skeptical assumptions.

senses.definition: In Orthodox and Catholic belief, the teaching and life of the Church handed down from the apostles, alongside Scripture.

core.definition: In Orthodox and Catholic belief, the teaching and life of the Church handed down from the apostles, alongside Scripture.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DISH in Tradition; the first syllable is a reduced 'truh.' Holy has a long o and the final y is a clear 'ee.'

nuance.connotation: Strongly positive in Orthodox and Catholic settings, where it means a living source of truth; sometimes contested by Protestants.
nuance.usage_note: Orthodox Christians often capitalize it as 'Holy Tradition' to mean the Church's whole living faith, including Scripture, creeds, councils, liturgy and the Fathers. Catholics more often say 'Sacred Tradition.'

distinctions.note: Lowercase tradition may be a human custom, while Holy Tradition is the divinely guided transmission of the faith.
Sacred Tradition is the usual Catholic term for the same idea.
Scripture is the written word; for Orthodox Christians it is the heart of Holy Tradition, not separate from it.

examples.everyday: My Orthodox friend explained that Holy Tradition includes the Bible, the liturgy and the Church Fathers.
examples.professional: In today's lecture, we'll look at how the Fathers understood Holy Tradition in the early Church.
examples.analytical: For Orthodox theology, Holy Tradition is not a second source beside Scripture but the Spirit-led life in which Scripture is read.

nuance.analogy: Like a river fed by many streams, not a separate lake from Scripture.
nuance.etymology: From Latin traditio, 'a handing over,' from tradere, 'to hand over.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable of Tradition.
Treating tradition only as old customs.
Thinking Orthodox and Catholics define it identically.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek paradosis means 'handing on.' 2 Thessalonians 2:15 urges believers to hold to the traditions taught by word or letter. 1 Corinthians 11:2 praises believers for holding fast to the traditions Paul delivered. 2 Timothy 2:2 speaks of entrusting teaching to faithful people who will teach others.

traditions.view: Holy Tradition is the Spirit-guided life of the whole Church, including Scripture, the creeds, councils, the Fathers, liturgy and icons; Scripture is its central part.
Sacred Tradition and Scripture form one deposit of faith, authentically interpreted by the Magisterium (Dei Verbum).
Generally holds that Scripture is the final authority and that tradition is subordinate; Anglicans and Lutherans value tradition more highly than many Baptists or Pentecostals.

senses.definition: An individual’s place of birth, childhood home, or place of main residence.
Designating a decision or judgment that is biased, or perceived to be biased, in favor of local preference.
senses.example: hometown decision, hometown verdict

core.definition: The town or city where a person was born or grew up, or where they mainly live.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on HOME, and the ow in town is a clear diphthong, like the ou in ouch. Keep the two words linked smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Positive or warm. It suggests roots, belonging and local pride.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use hometown in everyday small talk, such as 'Where's your hometown?' or 'I'm visiting my hometown this weekend.' Sports fans may also use hometown for home-team advantage, but that is a specific sense. The usual question for newcomers is 'Where are you from?' and an answer with a hometown name is natural.

distinctions.note: Hometown is the place where one was raised, while home can also mean the house where one currently lives.
Birthplace is the place where someone was born, which may differ from the town where they grew up.

examples.everyday: Where's your hometown? I think you said it's somewhere in Ohio, right?
examples.professional: Our hometown office in Ohio is hiring, so let me know if you want to transfer back.
examples.analytical: The novel treats the hometown as both a place of comfort and a source of constraint, which is typical of coming-of-age stories.

nuance.analogy: Like the first chapter of a book: it shapes everything that comes after, even when you move on.
nuance.etymology: Compound of home and town, from Old English ham and tun.
common_mistakes: Using hometown for any place you have visited, when it means where you grew up or live.
Writing home town as two words in formal writing, where American style prefers hometown.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Gospels, Jesus is rejected in his own town of Nazareth. Mark 6:4 in the Revised Standard Version says a prophet is not without honor except in his own country, showing how people struggle to accept someone familiar as a prophet. Luke 4:24 makes a similar point about a prophet not being accepted in his own country.

senses.definition: Of two or more liquids that are not mutually soluble: unmixable.
senses.example: A mixture of oil, water, and mercury forms three immiscible layers.

core.definition: Of liquids that do not mix or dissolve into each other, such as oil and water.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, -MIS-, not the first. The final syllable is a reduced bul, and the i at the start is a short ih, not ee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It describes a physical property with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use immiscible almost only in chemistry, chemical engineering, cooking science and lab work. In everyday talk they simply say oil and water do not mix. The opposite technical term is miscible, which describes liquids that mix freely. Use it precisely when writing lab reports or explaining chemistry.

distinctions.note: Insoluble describes a solid that does not dissolve; immiscible describes two liquids that do not mix.
Incompatible is broad and can describe people or systems; immiscible is strictly about liquids.

examples.everyday: Oil and water are immiscible, so the dressing separates into two layers in the bottle.
examples.professional: In the process design review, we noted that the two solvents are immiscible, so we need a separation step.
examples.analytical: The author uses immiscible liquids as a metaphor for two worldviews that cannot blend without one losing its identity.

nuance.analogy: Immiscible liquids are like people at a party who stay in separate groups and never fully mingle.
nuance.etymology: From Latin in- (not) and miscibilis (able to be mixed), from miscere (to mix).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as IM-is-si-ble; the stress is on the second syllable.
Confusing immiscible with inmiscible or with insoluble for solids.

senses.definition: Incapable of being physically moved: fixed.
Steadfast in purpose or intention: unalterable, unyielding.
Not capable of being affected or moved in feeling: impassive.
Not liable to be removed: permanent in place or tenure, fixed.
senses.example: an immovable estate

senses.definition: Something immovable.
Immovable objects or property, as land, buildings, etc.

core.definition: Impossible to move physically; or firm and unchanging in opinion, purpose, or feeling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'moo', not on the first. The -able ending is weak, so the final syllable sounds like 'bul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It can describe admirable firmness, or stubbornness and rigidity, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use immovable for physical objects that cannot be moved and for people who will not change their position. Calling someone immovable can be a criticism of stubbornness. In everyday speech Americans often say 'stubborn' or 'set in their ways' instead, and immovable sounds more formal.

distinctions.note: Stubborn is an everyday criticism of refusing to change; immovable is more formal and can describe firm principle as well as refusal.
Unmovable is a less common variant; immovable is the standard spelling in American English for both physical and figurative senses.

examples.everyday: My dad is immovable when it comes to politics; you could talk for hours and he would not change his mind.
examples.professional: Legal says the contract's deadline is immovable, so we need to shift the scope instead.
examples.analytical: Paul calls believers to be steadfast and immovable in the work of the Lord, because their labor is not in vain.

nuance.analogy: Like a mountain that does not move no matter how hard the wind blows.
nuance.etymology: From im- 'not' plus movable, from Latin movere 'to move'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable; the stress is on the second syllable, moo.
Confusing immovable with immobile, which usually refers to a living thing being unable to move.
nuance.biblical_note: In 1 Corinthians 15:58, the RSV urges believers to be steadfast and immovable in the work of the Lord. The Greek word is ametakinetos (immovable, unshaken), which describes a firm stability that does not waver under pressure. The passage links this steadfastness to the certainty of the resurrection, so the labor done for the Lord is not in vain.

senses.definition: Suggested indirectly, without being directly expressed; Implied.
senses.example: Poets often leave behind an implicit message within their words.

senses.definition: Contained in the essential nature of something but not openly shown.
Having no reservations or doubts; unquestioning or unconditional; usually said of faith or trust.

core.definition: Suggested or understood without being directly stated, or unquestioning, as in implicit trust.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'PLIS.' The final 'it' is short and reduced, so it is not 'im-PLEE-sit.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive when describing trust, and neutral when describing unstated meanings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'implicit' for unstated assumptions, as in 'an implicit agreement' or 'implicit bias.' In everyday speech 'unspoken' or 'understood' is common. 'Implicit trust' or 'implicit faith' is a natural, somewhat formal way to say someone trusts without question.

distinctions.note: 'Tacit' is closer to 'silently agreed,' often in formal agreements; 'implicit' can also mean included in the nature of something.
'Explicit' means clearly stated; 'implicit' means present but not stated.

examples.everyday: We never said we'd split the bill, but it was an implicit understanding between us.
examples.professional: Our model has an implicit assumption that customer behavior stays stable, so we should test that before launch.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on an implicit premise that moral obligation requires free choice, which the author never defends.

nuance.analogy: Like the foundation under a house, an implicit idea holds up the structure even though no one points at it.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin implicitus, past participle of implicare, 'to fold into, entangle.'
