senses.definition: A large pile of hay, grain, straw, or the like, larger at the bottom than the top, sometimes covered with thatch.
A pile of similar objects, each directly on top of the last.
senses.example: Please bring me a chair from that stack in the corner.

senses.definition: A pile of wood containing 108 cubic feet. (~3 m³)
An extensive collection.
A smokestack.
In computing.
senses.example: A TCP/IP stack is a library or set of libraries or of OS drivers that take care of networking.

senses.definition: A linear data structure in which items inserted are removed in reverse order (the last item inserted is the first one to be removed).
A stack data structure stored in main memory that is manipulated during machine language procedure call related instructions.
An implementation of a protocol suite (set of protocols forming a layered architecture).
senses.example: A TCP/IP stack is a library or set of libraries or of OS drivers that take care of networking.

senses.definition: A combination of interdependent, yet individually replaceable, software components or technologies used together on a system.
A generalization of schemes in algebraic geometry and of sheaves.
Compactly spaced bookshelves used to house large collections of books.
A large amount of an object.
senses.example: They paid him a stack of money to keep quiet.

senses.definition: The amount of money a player has on the table.
In architecture.
A number of flues embodied in one structure, rising above the roof.
A vertical drainpipe.
A blend of various dietary supplements or anabolic steroids with supposed synergistic benefits.
A holding pattern, with aircraft circling one above the other as they wait to land.
The quantity of a given item which fills up an inventory slot or bag.
senses.example: I've got 107 Golden Branches, but the stack size is 20 so they're taking up 6 spaces in my inventory.

senses.definition: A coastal landform, consisting of a large vertical column of rock in the sea.
A pile of rifles or muskets in a cone shape.
To arrange in a stack, or to add to an existing stack.
senses.example: Please stack those chairs in the corner.

senses.definition: To arrange the cards in a deck in a particular manner, especially for cheating.
senses.example: This is the third hand in a row where you've drawn four of a kind. Someone is stacking the deck!

senses.definition: To arrange or fix to obtain an advantage; to deliberately distort the composition of (an assembly, committee, etc.).
senses.example: to be stacked against (someone)

senses.definition: To take all the money another player currently has on the table.
senses.example: I won Jill's last $100 this hand; I stacked her!

senses.definition: To operate cumulatively.
senses.example: A magical widget will double your mojo. And yes, they do stack: if you manage to get two magical widgets, your mojo will be quadrupled. With three, it will be octupled, and so forth.

senses.definition: To place (aircraft) into a holding pattern.
To collect precious metal in the form of various small objects such as coins and bars.
To have excessive ink transfer.

core.definition: A neat pile of things placed one on top of another; in programming, a last-in, first-out data structure.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the short a of cat and a clear k at the end. Do not confuse it with stake, which is a different word with a long a.

nuance.connotation: neutral; a plain, practical word in everyday and technical use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stack for piles of plates, papers or pancakes, and in tech for layered systems, as in tech stack or call stack. In casual speech a stack of cash means a large amount of money. In software talk, people say the stack without thinking about the everyday meaning.

distinctions.note: A pile is more general and may be messy, while a stack is neat and arranged vertically.
In programming, a queue is first-in, first-out, while a stack is last-in, first-out.

examples.everyday: Can you put the clean plates in a stack on the counter so I can unload the dishwasher?
examples.professional: Our backend uses a Python stack running on a managed Kubernetes cluster.
examples.analytical: The interpreter keeps a stack of activation records, so each function call pushes a new frame onto it.

nuance.analogy: Like a stack of plates: you add to the top and take from the top.
nuance.etymology: From Old Norse stakkr, a haystack.
common_mistakes: Confusing stack with stake, which is a pointed post or a bet
Using stack for a single object; a stack needs at least two layered items

senses.definition: A person holding the stakes of bettors, with the responsibility of delivering the pot to the winner of the bet.
A person such as a trustee, escrow agent or garnishee, who holds money or assets under trust for another party in a contractual agreement or as part of a claim.
A person or organization with a legitimate interest (a stake) in a given situation, action or enterprise.
To involve stakeholders in (a project, process, decision, etc.).

core.definition: A person or group with an interest in or who is affected by a project, decision, or organization.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on STAYK, with a lighter secondary stress on hohl. The final syllable is a reduced American er, so do not say it as a full dur.

nuance.connotation: neutral to positive: it names people whose needs should be considered.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stakeholder constantly in business, government, and tech meetings, often in phrases like key stakeholders or stakeholder meeting. In casual talk, people say people who are affected or the people involved. Using it with friends can sound corporate, so save it for work.

distinctions.note: A shareholder owns stock in a company; a stakeholder may be anyone with an interest, including employees or customers.
A stakeholder in the business sense is a person with interest; the older sense means a person holding bets, which is rare now.

examples.everyday: My neighbors are the main stakeholders in the plan to widen the road, so they should get a say.
examples.professional: Before we launch, let's get feedback from all key stakeholders, including support and sales.
examples.analytical: A theory of responsibility must account for every stakeholder whose welfare the decision affects.

nuance.analogy: Like someone holding a share of the pot in a game: they have a stake in how the outcome turns out.
nuance.etymology: From stake, money wagered, plus holder, one who holds; originally a person holding wagers.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with shareholder, which has a narrower meaning.
Using it for any person; it implies a real interest or stake in the outcome.

conversation.text: We need to get all the stakeholders in a room before we decide.
Who are the key stakeholders for this project?
Let's send the draft to stakeholders for feedback by Wednesday.

senses.definition: A system in which typechecking is performed during compilation and not at run time, opposed to dynamic typing.

core.definition: A language design where variable types are checked during compilation, before the program runs, not while it runs.

pronunciation.tip: Both words have stress, with the main stress on TIE in typing. Say the -ing ending as 'ing', not 'een'.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It describes a design choice and is generally presented as a safety benefit.
nuance.usage_note: Engineers use static typing when comparing languages: Java and Go are statically typed, while Python is dynamically typed. A colleague might say 'static typing catches that bug before it ships.' The phrase is fixed and should not be altered.

distinctions.note: Dynamic typing checks types while the program runs, so errors appear later and only on the paths actually executed.
Strong typing describes how strictly types are enforced; static typing describes when they are checked, and the two are independent.

examples.everyday: My friend says static typing makes her code easier to trust, but I still like writing Python.
examples.professional: We moved the service to a statically typed language, and the compiler caught most of the null-reference errors.
examples.analytical: Static typing trades some expressive freedom for guarantees established before execution, a bargain whose value depends on the cost of late failure.

nuance.analogy: Static typing is like checking a passport at the gate before the flight, rather than discovering the problem after landing.
nuance.etymology: Static from Greek statikos, causing to stand; typing from Greek typos, impression or mold.
common_mistakes: Thinking static typing means variables cannot change value; it concerns when types are checked
Pronouncing the first word as 'STAH-tic'

senses.definition: Rigid; hard to bend; inflexible.
Inflexible; rigid.
Formal in behavior; unrelaxed.
Harsh, severe.
senses.example: He was eventually caught, and given a stiff fine.

senses.definition: Painful or more rigid than usual as a result of excessive or unaccustomed exercise.
senses.example: My legs are stiff after climbing that hill yesterday.

senses.definition: Potent.
senses.example: a stiff drink; a stiff dose; a stiff breeze

senses.definition: Expensive, pricey.
Dead, deceased.
Erect.
Having a dense consistency; thick; Difficult to stir.
senses.example: Adding too much peanut butter to your Peanut Sauce recipe may cause your sauce to turn out too stiff.

senses.definition: Beaten until so aerated that they stand up straight on their own.
senses.example: beat the egg whites until they are stiff

senses.definition: Of an equation, for which certain numerical solving methods are numerically unstable, unless the step size is taken to be extremely small.
Of a shot, landing so close to the flagstick that it should be very easy to sink the ball with the next shot.
Delivered more forcefully than needed, whether intentionally or accidentally, thus causing legitimate pain to the opponent.
Keeping upright.
An average person, usually male, of no particular distinction, skill, or education.
senses.example: working stiff

senses.definition: A person who is deceived, as a mark or pigeon in a swindle.
senses.example: She convinced the stiff to go to her hotel room, where her henchman was waiting to rob him.

senses.definition: A cadaver; a dead person.
A flop; a commercial failure.
A person who leaves (especially a restaurant) without paying the bill.
A customer who does not leave a tip.
Any hard hand where it is possible to exceed 21 by drawing an additional card.
Negotiable instruments, possibly forged.
A note or letter surreptitiously sent by an inmate.
To fail to pay that which one owes (implicitly or explicitly) to another, especially by departing hastily.
senses.example: He stiffed me on the tip.

senses.definition: To cheat someone.
To tip ungenerously.
To kill.
To be unsuccessful.
Of the wind, with great force; strongly.
Very thoroughly.

core.definition: Hard to bend or move; rigid. Also describes a person or manner that is formal and not relaxed.

pronunciation.tip: Short i as in 'sit' and a crisp final f with no extra vowel after it. Non-native speakers often add a schwa, saying 'stiff-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for physical stiffness; mildly negative when describing people or manners, suggesting coldness or lack of ease.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'I'm stiff' after a workout or a long flight, meaning sore and tight. For manners, 'stiff' suggests someone is uptight or formal, so it can sound unfriendly when used about a host or colleague. A common casual reply to 'How are you doing?' after exercise is 'Sore and stiff, but good.'

distinctions.note: Rigid suggests something that cannot bend at all, often by design; stiff is more often a temporary or partial quality, as in stiff muscles.
Formal describes proper behavior in a situation; stiff describes a feeling of awkwardness or lack of relaxation in that behavior.

examples.everyday: I'm so stiff from raking leaves all afternoon.
examples.professional: The meeting felt stiff at first, but people loosened up after the first presentation.
examples.analytical: A stiff bureaucratic style can signal distance rather than competence, and readers often notice that gap.

nuance.analogy: A stiff brush has bristles that won't bend, like a new pair of jeans that has not been broken in.
nuance.etymology: From Old English stif, meaning unyielding or firm.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel, saying 'stiff-uh'.
Using stiff to mean only very firm in food; Americans prefer 'thick' or 'firm' for food.

stiff.etymology: From Middle English *stiff*, *stiffe*, *stif*, from Old English *stīf*, from **stīf*, from Proto-Germanic **stīfaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **steypós*.

senses.definition: A pushing or goading toward action.
An activity causing excitement or pleasure; the act of stimulating.
Any action or condition that creates a response; sensory input.

core.definition: The act of stimulating something, or an activity or condition that makes a person or thing more active, interested, or excited.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on LAY, and the -ate in the verb stimulate drops to a weak syllable in stimulation. Don't pronounce the middle syllable as a full 'yoo' sound; it is a quick 'yuh'.

nuance.connotation: Usually positive or neutral. It can be positive (mental stimulation, a lively discussion) or neutral to negative when it means overstimulation or excessive sensory input.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stimulation for mental challenge ('kids need mental stimulation'), for sensory input ('too much stimulation can overwhelm a toddler'), and in economics ('stimulation of the economy' or 'economic stimulus'). In casual speech people more often say 'it's exciting' or 'a lot going on'. A natural reply to a compliment on a lively event is 'Yeah, there was a lot of stimulation.'

distinctions.note: Stimulation is the process or the resulting activity; a stimulus is the specific thing that triggers the response.
Motivation is the internal reason to act, while stimulation is an external force or activity that increases energy or interest.

examples.everyday: My dog gets bored fast, so I give him puzzle toys for mental stimulation.
examples.professional: The new onboarding plan adds more stimulation for junior analysts, so fewer of them leave in the first year.
examples.analytical: Aristotle treats the stimulation of the senses as the first step toward understanding, not the whole of knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Stimulation is like a coach's whistle for the mind: it gets things moving, but it does not decide where the team runs.
nuance.etymology: From Latin stimulare, to goad or prick, from stimulus.
common_mistakes: Using stimulation as a countable noun for a single event (say 'a stimulus' or 'an activity').
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying stim-yoo-LAY-shun with the stress on the first syllable only.

senses.definition: To be sparing or mean.
senses.example: The next party you throw, don't stint on the beer.

senses.definition: To restrain within certain limits; to bound; to restrict to a scant allowance.
To assign a certain task to (a person), upon the performance of which he/she is excused from further labor for that day or period; to stent.
To impregnate successfully; to get with foal.
A period of time spent doing or being something; a spell.
senses.example: He had a stint in jail.

senses.definition: Limit; bound; restraint; extent.
Quantity or task assigned; proportion allotted.
A part of the race between two consecutive pit stops.
Any of several very small wading birds in the genus Calidris. Types of sandpiper, such as the dunlin or the sanderling.

core.definition: A fixed period of time spent doing a particular job or activity, such as a work shift or military tour.

pronunciation.tip: Use a short 'ih' vowel and end with a clear nt sound. Do not add a 'd' or 'k' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a period of work or service without judgment, though context can make it feel tiring or hard.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stint for a period of work or service, such as 'a two-year stint in the Army' or 'a stint at a startup'. It is common in both casual and professional talk. For a very short job, people may say 'a short stint'. Do not confuse it with stink.

distinctions.note: Spell is more general and can mean a short period of any kind; stint usually refers to a job or assigned period of work.
Tour often refers to a formal duty period, especially military, while stint can apply to any job.

examples.everyday: My brother did a stint in the Navy before he went to college.
examples.professional: She did a three-year stint on the data platform team before moving to product.
examples.analytical: Her stint as a parish administrator shaped her view of institutional authority.

nuance.analogy: A stint is like a single shift on a long ride: it has a clear start and end, and it is one part of the whole journey.
nuance.etymology: From Old English stintan, to stop or make blunt, later to limit.
common_mistakes: Confusing stint (a period of work) with stink (a bad smell).
Using stint for a permanent job; it implies a limited period.

stint.etymology: From Middle English *stinten*, from Old English *styntan* (“to make blunt”) and **stintan* (attested in *āstintan* (“to make dull, stint, assuage”)), from **stuntijan*, from Proto-Germanic **stuntijaną* and Proto-Germanic **stintaną* (“to make short”),…

senses.definition: Money to spend at a store, given instead of a refund.

core.definition: Money that a store gives you as a credit to spend there later, usually instead of paying back cash.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on CRED, and the middle t in CREDIT is a quick flap that sounds like a soft 'd.' Do not pronounce the second syllable as 'deet.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be a helpful option but can also feel like a limitation if you wanted cash.
nuance.usage_note: In American stores, you may hear 'We can give you store credit' when a return has no receipt or when the store has a no-cash-refund policy. A natural reply is 'Store credit is fine' or 'Can I get a refund to my card instead?' Americans often ask about the store's return policy before accepting it.

distinctions.note: Store credit is usually issued after a return and is tied to your account, while a gift card is a prepaid card you buy for someone.
A refund returns your original money, while store credit can only be spent at that store.

examples.everyday: They gave me store credit for the shirt because I didn't have the receipt.
examples.professional: Finance flagged that our return policy issues store credit rather than cash, which affects how we book refund liabilities.
examples.analytical: Store credit keeps the customer's money inside the retailer, which benefits the business even when it appears to be a concession to the buyer.

nuance.analogy: Store credit is like a coupon with a large balance: the value is real, but it only works in one place.
nuance.etymology: 'Store' from Old French estore and 'credit' from Latin creditum, something entrusted.
common_mistakes: Using 'store credit' to mean a loan from a store, which is a different meaning in some contexts.
Pronouncing CREDIT as 'cred-it' with a hard t instead of a flap.

conversation.text: Without a receipt, we can only give you store credit.
I still have store credit from returning my holiday gifts.
Would you prefer a refund or store credit?

senses.definition: Auxiliary or supplemental.
Secondary or subordinate.
senses.example: a subsidiary stream

senses.definition: Of or relating to a subsidy.
senses.example: subsidiary payments to an ally

senses.definition: A company owned by a parent company or a holding company, also called daughter company or sister company.
One who aids or supplies; an assistant.
A subordinate theme.

core.definition: A company that is owned and controlled by a larger parent company, which holds most or all of its shares.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SID, the second syllable. The final syllables are reduced, so say air-ee rather than the full ary ending, and do not add an extra syllable as in sub-SIJ-ee-ar-ee.

nuance.connotation: neutral, a precise business term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use subsidiary as a business term for a company owned by a larger company, such as a brand that belongs to a conglomerate. In everyday conversation people might say 'it's a subsidiary of' or 'a division of.' The adjective sense, meaning secondary or supporting, appears in formal writing, as in 'a subsidiary role.'

distinctions.note: A division is a part of the same company, while a subsidiary is a separate legal company controlled by the parent.
An affiliate is related to a company through partial ownership or other ties, while a subsidiary is majority owned and controlled.

examples.everyday: That grocery brand is actually a subsidiary of a much bigger food company, which I didn't know.
examples.professional: Our European subsidiary will report its quarterly results to the parent company in New York next week.
examples.analytical: The legal separation between a subsidiary and its parent raises questions about corporate responsibility when harm occurs.

nuance.analogy: A subsidiary is like a branch of a family tree that keeps its own name and legal identity but still answers to the main trunk.
nuance.etymology: From Latin subsidiarius, of reserve troops, from subsidium, reserve force.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing subsidiary with extra syllables, such as sub-SIJ-ee-ar-ee, instead of sub-SID-ee-air-ee.
Using subsidiary to mean a division inside the same company; a subsidiary is a separate legal entity.

subsidiary.etymology: From Middle French *subsidiaire*, from Latin *subsidiarius* (“belonging to a reserve”).

senses.definition: The quality or state of being superfluous; overflowingness.
Something superfluous, such as a luxury.
A group of nuns.

core.definition: An excess amount of something beyond what is needed, or something that is unnecessary.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -floo-, so say soo-per-FLOO-uh-tee. The -ity ending is pronounced tee, and the middle syllables reduce quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, suggesting waste or excess beyond need.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use superfluity in everyday talk; they say "extra" or "too much." It appears in formal writing, essays, and sometimes in discussions of luxury or waste. Using it in casual conversation would sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Surplus usually means a useful extra amount that can be used later, while superfluity suggests an unnecessary or wasteful excess.
Excess is the more common everyday word for too much, while superfluity is more formal and stresses that the extra is unneeded.

examples.everyday: We had a superfluity of pizza at the party, so I took home two boxes.
examples.professional: The budget review found a superfluity of software licenses that nobody on the team was using.
examples.analytical: The author's prose suffers from a superfluity of adjectives that obscure rather than clarify the argument.

nuance.analogy: A superfluity is like a closet stuffed with clothes you never wear: far more than you need, and the extra only gets in the way.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin superfluitas, from superfluus (overflowing), from super (above) and fluere (to flow).
common_mistakes: Using superfluity as a countable noun; it is usually uncountable, as in a superfluity of.
Confusing it with superfluous, the adjective.

superfluity.etymology: From *superfluous* + *ity*, Old French *superfluite*, from Medieval Latin *superfluitas*, from Latin *superfluus*.

senses.definition: To take the place of.
senses.example: Those older products have been superseded by our new range.

senses.definition: To displace in favor of itself.
senses.example: Modern US culture has superseded the native forms.

senses.definition: An updated newsgroup post that supersedes an earlier version.
senses.example: Rogue cancels and supersedes are being issued on a large scale against posters.

core.definition: To take the place of something earlier, making it outdated, obsolete, or no longer valid.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the final syllable, SEED. The first syllable and the middle syllable are quick and reduced, and the final sound is a long e, not a short i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes replacement and can sound slightly formal or official.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use supersede in business, law, software, and policy: 'This version supersedes the previous one.' In casual talk people more often say 'replace' or 'take over from.' It is a common term in workplace email and documentation.

distinctions.note: Replace is everyday and neutral. Supersede implies the new thing is better or newer and makes the old one invalid.
Succeed means to come after someone in a role. Supersede means to replace something that is no longer valid or effective.

examples.everyday: My old phone plan is gone now, because the new one supersedes it.
examples.professional: This new guideline supersedes the one from last year, so please update your team's documentation today.
examples.analytical: Hegel's dialectic does not simply discard earlier positions but supersedes them by preserving what each one got right.

nuance.analogy: To supersede is like a new chapter that rewrites the old one: the earlier text is no longer the official version.
nuance.etymology: From Latin supersedere, 'to sit above, refrain from,' from super, 'above,' and sedere, 'to sit.'
common_mistakes: Using supersede with a preposition, as in 'supersede to,' when the verb takes a direct object.
Pronouncing it with the stress on the first syllable, as in 'SU-per-seed.'

supersede.etymology: From Middle French *superseder* (“postpone, defer”), from Latin *supersedeo*, from *super* (“over”) + *sedeo* (“to sit”).

senses.definition: To oversee or direct (a task or organization).
senses.example: Without someone to supervise them, the group will lack direction.

senses.definition: To oversee a task, organization, etc. to provide supervision; to act as a supervisor.

core.definition: To watch over and direct the work of others, making sure that tasks are done correctly and on time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, SOO. The middle syllable is a weak r-vowel, and the final -ise is pronounced like 'eyes' with a z sound.

nuance.connotation: neutral. The word describes a job or role; it can sound controlling when used of a manager who watches too closely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use supervise for the daily oversight of employees, students, interns, or construction work. In an office you might say 'Who supervises you?' For a more casual idea, Americans often say 'oversee' or 'be in charge of'. Supervise is also used in academia: a professor supervises a dissertation. In everyday talk, 'watch' or 'keep an eye on' is more natural for children or pets.

distinctions.note: Oversee is broader and more general, covering a whole project from above; supervise suggests direct, hands-on watching of the people doing the work.
Manage covers planning, budgets and results; supervise focuses on the daily work and workers being watched.

examples.everyday: My sister supervises the night shift at a bakery, so she's always up early.
examples.professional: I supervise two data engineers, so please send your questions about the pipeline to me or to them directly.
examples.analytical: A good academic institution must balance the freedom of scholars with the duty to supervise their research ethically.

nuance.analogy: Like a lifeguard on a crowded beach, watching the swimmers so the work stays safe and on track.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin supervisus, past participle of supervidere 'to oversee', from super 'over' and videre 'to see'.
common_mistakes: Adding a preposition: say 'supervise the team', not 'supervise over the team'.
Stressing the second syllable (su-PER-vise); the stress is on SOO.

senses.definition: Having no tact; unaware or intentionally inconsiderate of someone else's feelings.
senses.example: It was tactless of you not to attend your sister's wedding.

core.definition: Saying or doing things that hurt or embarrass people because one does not think about their feelings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the 'ct' clearly. The final syllable is a reduced 'us' sound, not 'ess.'

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes someone for hurting others by careless speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tactless to describe a remark or person who said something hurtful without thinking, such as 'That was tactless of him to bring up her divorce.' It is common in everyday conversation and in workplace feedback. Calling someone tactless directly can be harsh, so people often soften it with 'a bit tactless.'

distinctions.note: Rude means deliberately impolite; tactless means careless about feelings, often without intending harm.
Blunt describes honest, direct speech; tactless describes speech that ignores how it will affect the listener.

examples.everyday: That was a tactless thing to say at the funeral, honestly.
examples.professional: Asking the candidate about her age in the interview was tactless and could create legal problems.
examples.analytical: The narrator's tactless honesty exposes the gap between truthfulness and kindness.

nuance.analogy: A tactless remark is like stepping on someone's toe while trying to reach for the door: you did not mean to hurt them, but you did.
nuance.etymology: From tact plus the suffix -less, meaning 'without.'
common_mistakes: Using tactless to mean 'dishonest'; it describes a lack of sensitivity, not a lack of truthfulness.
Using 'tactless' for 'impolite' in a deliberate insult, where 'rude' is more accurate.

senses.definition: A Levite of the Kohathite line, named among the ancestors in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, linked to the family of the temple musicians.

core.definition: A Levite of the Kohathite line, named among the ancestors in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, linked to the family of the temple musicians.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and pronounce the 'th' at the end as in 'bath.' Don't add an extra vowel after the 'h.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a name in Scripture with no evaluative meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Tahath is a biblical name used mainly in Bible study, scholarly discussion, and church reading. Americans would not use it in everyday conversation. Readers often encounter it in genealogy lists, where they can skip it without losing the thread.

distinctions.note: Tahath is a person's name in the genealogies, while Tahpanhes is a city in Egypt.

examples.everyday: In the Bible study group, someone asked who Tahath was, and we found him in the genealogy of Levi.
examples.professional: In the commentary on 1 Chronicles, Tahath is treated as one name in the Kohathite line of Levitical ancestors.
examples.analytical: The genealogical lists of Tahath reflect the effort to preserve Levitical lineage for temple service.

nuance.analogy: Tahath is like a name on a family tree that shows how one branch connects to another.
common_mistakes: Confusing Tahath with Tahpanhes, which is a city.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: Tahath appears as a Levite of the Kohathite family in the genealogies, which trace the lineage of temple service. He is named in 1 Chronicles 6:24 among the descendants of Kohath, and another Tahath, an Ephraimite, is named in 1 Chronicles 7:19. In these passages the name serves to record family lines rather than to tell a narrative about Tahath himself.

senses.definition: Discuss something later, outside the meeting, with fewer people.

core.definition: To move a discussion out of the current meeting to a later, smaller conversation.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on OFF, with secondary stress on LINE. Note that 'offline' is pronounced with a full ow-like vowel, not 'off-lyn', and the t in 'it' is often a flap.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American workplaces, especially tech companies, this phrase is used when a debate is taking too long or includes too many people. A typical reply is 'Sure, let's sync after the meeting.' It can sound slightly managerial, so use it politely.

distinctions.vs: take it up after the meeting
distinctions.note: Both mean discuss later; 'take it offline' is more jargon-heavy and common in tech.
'Table it' means postpone without a set time; 'take it offline' implies a separate follow-up conversation.

examples.everyday: We're arguing about dinner plans in front of everyone, so let's take it offline later.
examples.professional: This debate about the API design is taking too long, so let's take it offline and include only the owners.
examples.analytical: Rather than settle the dispute in plenary, the committee chose to take it offline to a smaller working group.

nuance.analogy: Like moving a loud argument from the living room into the kitchen with only the people who need to be there.
common_mistakes: Using 'offline' only as 'not connected to the internet'; in meetings it means outside the meeting.
Saying 'take it off-line' with a hyphen in speech, which is unnatural.

conversation.text: This is getting into the details. Can we take it offline?
Let's take it offline so we don't hold up the whole group.
James and I will take it offline and report back.

senses.definition: To discuss; to converse about a matter or issue.
senses.example: Come home early, we have a lot to talk over.

senses.definition: To verbally interrupt (someone); to speak at the same time as someone else.
senses.example: She rudely talked over her opponent in the debate.

senses.definition: To persuade (someone); to talk around.
senses.example: I didn't like the idea at first, but they eventually talked me over.

core.definition: To discuss a matter with someone, especially to reach a decision; also, to interrupt someone by speaking while they are still talking.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle 'over' (OH-ver), and say the final syllable as a reduced American 'er', not 'ow-ver'. The 'v' is voiced, linking smoothly to the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when meaning 'discuss'; negative when meaning 'interrupt' or 'drown out', because it suggests someone is not being listened to.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, 'let's talk it over' is a common, friendly way to suggest discussing a problem before deciding. The sense 'talk over someone' means to keep speaking while someone else is trying to talk, and Americans often find this rude, especially in meetings. Context makes the meaning clear.

distinctions.note: 'Discuss' is more formal and direct; 'talk over' is casual and often implies a personal, relaxed conversation about a decision.
'Interrupt' means breaking in; 'talk over' specifically means continuing to speak loudly while another person is speaking.

examples.everyday: Let's talk it over tonight and decide whether we should move closer to your parents.
examples.professional: Can we talk over the migration plan with the infrastructure team before we send the change request?
examples.analytical: Hobbes suggests that when people talk over one another in public debate, reasoned argument gives way to the loudest voice.

nuance.analogy: Like two people passing a ball of ideas back and forth until they settle on one.
nuance.etymology: From 'talk' plus 'over', meaning across or through a matter, from Old English ofer.
common_mistakes: Using 'talk over' for a simple 'talk about' in formal writing, where 'discuss' is more natural.
Forgetting that 'talk over someone' is rude in American meetings; it is better to say 'Sorry, go ahead' or 'Can I finish?'

conversation.text: Let's talk it over at lunch tomorrow.
We talked over the offer before I accepted it.
Stop talking over me; let me finish.

senses.definition: Someone who supervises workers, especially one who imposes hard or burdensome work.
A source of hard work or responsibility.
Someone who is capable of performing many tasks; a multitasker.

core.definition: A person who demands hard work from others, often in a strict or harsh way, or who pushes others to complete difficult tasks.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -er is a reduced American r sound. Keep the secondary stress light on master.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests someone who is strict, demanding or harsh, though it can be used more lightly for a coach or manager.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use taskmaster for bosses, coaches or parents who push people hard. It can be half-joking, as in 'My trainer is a real taskmaster.' It is usually not a compliment unless the speaker wants to praise discipline. In a workplace, describing someone as a taskmaster can suggest that they are demanding but effective.

distinctions.note: Boss is a general word for a supervisor, while taskmaster specifically highlights demanding, strict control over work.
Supervisor is neutral and formal, while taskmaster carries a strong sense of pressure and hardship.

examples.everyday: My gym coach is a real taskmaster, but I feel stronger every week.
examples.professional: Our manager is a taskmaster about deadlines, so the team always delivers on time.
examples.analytical: The author describes the economy as a taskmaster that drives people past their natural limits.

nuance.analogy: A taskmaster is like a coach with a whistle who never lets the team rest.
nuance.etymology: From task plus master, meaning one who sets and enforces tasks.
common_mistakes: Using taskmaster for a friendly teacher without the sense of pressure.
Writing it as two words, task master, in formal writing where the single compound is standard.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Old Testament, taskmasters are the Egyptian overseers who forced the Israelites to do hard labor. The Hebrew word is nogesh, meaning an overseer or driver of workers. Exodus 1:11 says Egypt set taskmasters over Israel to afflict them with burdens, and Exodus 3:7 describes God hearing the cry of his people because of their taskmasters. Exodus 5:6 shows Pharaoh ordering the taskmasters to stop giving straw to the people.

senses.definition: Reckless boldness; foolish bravery.
An act or case of reckless boldness.
Effrontery; impudence.

core.definition: Reckless boldness, or the nerve to do something risky or rude without regard for consequences, often in a way that seems disrespectful.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MEH, and the first syllable is a weak schwa. The final -ity is usually a soft 'tee' or a flapped 'dee' in fast speech, not a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that someone was bold in a way others found presumptuous or foolish, though it can sound admiring in a wry way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use temerity mostly in writing, news commentary, and formal speech, rather than in casual conversation. You might hear someone say he had the temerity to do something when they are annoyed. The everyday American equivalent is nerve or gall, as in he had the nerve to ask for a raise.

distinctions.note: Audacity can be admired as daring and creative, while temerity usually suggests recklessness or disrespect.
Nerve is informal and everyday, and it often describes courage in a tense moment; temerity is more formal and always carries some criticism.
Courage is a moral strength aimed at a good end, while temerity is boldness that is careless about danger or others' feelings.

examples.everyday: He had the temerity to ask my sister for a loan on their first date.
examples.professional: It took real temerity to propose cutting the pilot before we had any results.
examples.analytical: Critics of the argument questioned the temerity of claiming certainty about causes that experience can never fully confirm.

nuance.analogy: Like a driver who speeds through a red light because he assumes no one will stop him, temerity is confidence that ignores the real risk.
nuance.etymology: From Latin temeritas, meaning rashness or chance, from temere, meaning blindly or by chance.
common_mistakes: Using temerity as a synonym for courage in a positive sense; it usually criticizes the boldness.
Stressing the first syllable (TEM-uh-ruh-tee) instead of the second.

temerity.etymology: From Middle English *temerite*, *temeryte*, from Old French *temerité*, from Latin *temeritās* (“chance, accident, rashness”), from *temere* (“by chance, casually, rashly”).

senses.definition: Partaking of, or combining, both divinity and humanity.

core.definition: Combining both divine and human nature or qualities in one being.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on the -throp- syllable, with weaker stress on the first syllable. Both 'th' sounds are voiceless, and the final -ic is short /ɪk/, not /aɪk/.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a specialized theological term that is not used in ordinary talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it mainly in theology, seminary study, and Eastern Orthodox writing about Christ's union of God and man. You may also see it in literary writing about hybrid or mythic beings. In everyday speech, say 'fully divine and fully human' instead.

distinctions.note: 'Divine' describes only God, while 'theanthropic' stresses the union of God and humanity in one being.
'Incarnate' means embodied in flesh and can be used loosely for ideas or qualities, while 'theanthropic' is a precise technical term about two natures.

examples.everyday: My priest said the Incarnation is a theanthropic mystery, so I'm still trying to wrap my head around it.
examples.professional: In the seminary lecture, the professor described Christ's theanthropic person as the foundation for the doctrine of salvation.
examples.analytical: Maximus the Confessor's account of the theanthropic union preserves both the full divinity and the full humanity of Christ without confusion.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin that is both metal and money at once, one object with two natures.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theos (god) and anthrōpos (human being).
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'anthropic' (relating to human existence in cosmology); the prefix 'thea-' is what makes it theological.
Stressing the 'an' syllable; the primary stress is on '-throp-'.

senses.definition: A person who has a personal knowledge of God through prayer, asceticism, and mystical experience.
A specialist in academic theology.
Someone who studies theology.
senses.example: Seminarians are usually divided into philosophers and theologians, depending on their stage of formation.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) A theological lecturer attached to a cathedral church.

core.definition: A person who studies or writes about God and religious beliefs, usually as a trained scholar or teacher of theology.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LOH, and the -gian ending is a reduced schwa plus n, so it sounds like 'jun,' not 'gee-an.' The first syllable can sound like 'thee-uh' in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a respected scholar or a trained expert, though some believers may use the word more loosely for any thoughtful person who writes about faith.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use theologian for professors at seminaries and divinity schools, and for authors of books on Christian doctrine. In everyday talk, people often say he's a theologian to mean he thinks deeply about God, usually with a little admiration. The word is used across denominations, but Catholics and Orthodox often apply it more narrowly to people with formal training or authority.

distinctions.note: A pastor leads and cares for a congregation, while a theologian focuses on study and teaching of doctrine, though one person can be both.
A philosopher of religion analyzes religious concepts with general philosophical tools, while a theologian works within a particular faith tradition and its sources.

examples.everyday: My friend Mark is a theologian at the seminary, so I always ask him about faith questions over coffee.
examples.professional: We invited a theologian from the divinity school to speak to the church staff about the new study curriculum.
examples.analytical: The theologian argues that divine omniscience and human freedom must be understood together rather than as competing claims.

nuance.analogy: A theologian is like a structural engineer for belief: they examine how the parts of doctrine hold together and where the load-bearing beams are.
nuance.etymology: From Greek theologos, 'one who speaks of God,' from theos 'god' and logos 'word, discourse.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'theologist,' which is rare and sounds unnatural; use theologian.
Stressing the wrong syllable as 'thee-uh-LOH-jee-un' instead of ending with a short 'jun' sound.

traditions.view: Orthodox tradition uses theologian in a deeper sense, for someone who knows God through prayer and purification, as in the title 'John the Theologian.' Formal academic study is valued but is not the main test.
A theologian is usually a trained scholar who works in service to the Church's teaching, and the magisterium holds final authority over official doctrine.

Protestants generally see a theologian as accountable to Scripture and the community of faith, with authority varying by denomination; Reformed, Lutheran, Baptist and Anglican scholars often differ on method and emphasis.

senses.definition: Of, or relating to a transition.
senses.example: transitional justice

senses.definition: Temporary; pending the implementation of something new.
senses.example: XHTML 1.0 Transitional

core.definition: Relating to a change from one state or condition to another; temporary while something new is put in place.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZISH, and the -shun- syllable is reduced to uh. The final -al is a light, quick -ul, with no separate vowel sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests change in progress and can be positive when it means growth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use transitional in speech about life phases, policies, housing, and jobs, as in transitional housing or a transitional period. It sounds more formal than in-between. It is a common term in education and social services.

distinctions.note: Transitory emphasizes brevity and passing away; transitional emphasizes being a bridge between two states.
Interim describes a temporary position or arrangement; transitional more often describes a process of change.

examples.everyday: We are in a transitional phase right now since I just moved to Denver and started a new job.
examples.professional: Our transitional plan keeps the old API running until every client migrates to version two.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the modern self as a transitional figure, caught between tradition and secular individualism.

nuance.analogy: A transitional phase is like a bridge: you are not on either bank yet, but you are clearly crossing.
nuance.etymology: From transition, from Latin transitio, a going across.
common_mistakes: Stressing the -shun- syllable instead of ZISH
Using transitional to mean only temporary, when it stresses change between states

senses.definition: Trembling with fear or emotion.

core.definition: Nervous or fearful, trembling with anxiety or apprehension about what may happen.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowels are reduced, so the word has three quick syllables, with the final 'ant' weakened to 'dunt'.

nuance.connotation: negative; it describes fear or anxiety.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use trepidant in speech. It appears occasionally in literary writing or deliberately old-fashioned prose. In everyday American English, say 'nervous', 'anxious' or 'apprehensive'. The more common related word is trepidatious, which is informal and playful.

distinctions.note: Trepidant is an adjective describing a person in a fearful state, while trepidation is a noun for the feeling itself.
Apprehensive is common and neutral in tone; trepidant is rare, literary and more emotionally vivid.

examples.everyday: She sounded a little trepidant when she called to ask about the test results.
examples.professional: The trepidant team waited for the audit report, unsure what it would reveal.
examples.analytical: The trepidant narrator of the novel hesitates at every threshold, unable to trust his own perceptions.

nuance.analogy: A trepidant person is like a leaf shaking in the wind before a storm, moved by a fear that has not yet arrived.
nuance.etymology: From Latin trepidans, present participle of trepidare, to be alarmed.
common_mistakes: Using trepidant in casual conversation, where 'nervous' is far more natural.
Confusing trepidant (adjective) with trepidation (noun), as in 'She felt trepidant' instead of 'She felt trepidation'.

senses.definition: Being everywhere at once: omnipresent.
senses.example: In Christianity, Hinduism, and Judaism, God is ubiquitous.

senses.definition: Appearing to be everywhere at once; being or seeming to be in more than one location at the same time.
Widespread; very prevalent.

core.definition: Present or found everywhere at the same time, or very widespread, so that it seems to be all around.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, BIK, and reduce the final syllables to a short 'us'. The kw is a clear consonant cluster, so say it as one smooth sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, depending on the context; it can describe useful things everywhere or unwanted things that are too common.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ubiquitous in business, technology, and news writing, such as describing smartphones or advertising. In casual speech they often say everywhere or all over the place. It can sound a little formal in conversation, but it is natural in professional writing.

distinctions.note: Omnipresent is a stronger, more formal word often used for God or for an unavoidable presence, while ubiquitous describes widespread presence in ordinary contexts.
Common means frequently found or usual, but ubiquitous suggests it is found almost everywhere at once.

examples.everyday: Coffee shops are ubiquitous in this neighborhood, so I never have to walk far for a latte.
examples.professional: Cloud computing has become ubiquitous in our data infrastructure, so every team now relies on it.
examples.analytical: Scholars argue that the ubiquitous presence of the market shapes how people understand personal value.

nuance.analogy: Something ubiquitous is like the air around us: it is so present everywhere that we barely notice it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ubique, meaning everywhere, from ubi, where.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (YOO-bik-wih-tus); the stress belongs on BIK.
Pronouncing the kw as k only, which drops a sound and makes the word harder to hear.

ubiquitous.etymology: From *ubiquity* + *ous*, from Medieval Latin *ubīquitās*, from Latin *ubīque* (“everywhere”), from *ubī̆* (“where”) + *-que* (“each, ever”).

senses.definition: A final statement of terms or conditions made by one party to another, especially one that expresses a threat of reprisal or war if the terms are not met before some specified date and time.
An intended final statement of terms or conditions made by one party to another in a negotiation.

core.definition: A final demand or set of conditions from one party, with a threat of serious consequences if the other side does not comply by a set deadline.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on MAY, with a weaker secondary stress on the first syllable. The middle t is lightly flapped, so it sounds close to a d, and the final syllable is a weak um, not tum with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative or tense. An ultimatum signals pressure and possible conflict, so it is used seriously rather than casually.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ultimatum in news, politics, labor disputes and family conflicts when someone sets a firm deadline with consequences. In casual talk people often say 'I'm not kidding, this is my last offer' instead. The verb form 'give someone an ultimatum' is the most common way to use it.

distinctions.note: A demand is a request for something; an ultimatum is a demand with a deadline and a threat attached.
A deadline is a time limit for finishing work; an ultimatum is a threat that follows if the deadline is missed.

examples.everyday: My sister gave me an ultimatum: either I pay back the money by Friday or she will stop speaking to me.
examples.professional: The union issued an ultimatum to management, demanding a pay increase by Monday or a strike would begin.
examples.analytical: Coercive diplomacy relies on the ultimatum, which makes compliance the only alternative to a threatened cost.

nuance.analogy: An ultimatum is like a closing door: you are told to walk through it now, or it shuts behind you.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ultimatum, neuter past participle of ultimare 'to come to an end', from ultimus 'last'.
common_mistakes: Using the plural as 'ultimatums' correctly, but treating it as an adjective; it is only a noun.
Mispronouncing the final syllable as a strong 'tum' rather than a weak 'tum' with a reduced vowel.

ultimatum.etymology: From Latin *ultimatus* (“late, last final”), from Latin *ultimus* (“extreme, last, furthest, farthest, final”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to a majuscule style of writing with unjoined, rounded letters, originally used in the 4th–9th centuries.
Of or relating to an ounce, or an inch, especially to letters printed an inch high.
A style of writing using uncial letters.
A letter in this style.
A manuscript in this style.

core.definition: Relating to an early style of capital-like handwriting with rounded, unjoined letters, used in ancient manuscripts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, UN. The c is pronounced like 'sh' before the i, so the word sounds like 'UN-shul', not 'UN-see-al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized term used by historians, paleographers, and textual scholars.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use uncial almost only in academic, museum, or religious-scholarship contexts. Most people would not know the word, so explain it when you use it. It is common in discussions of early Bible manuscripts such as Codex Sinaiticus.

distinctions.note: Majuscule is the general term for capital-style writing, while uncial is a specific rounded majuscule style from roughly the 4th to 9th centuries.
Minuscule refers to lowercase letters, while uncial refers to a style of capital letters.

examples.everyday: That old book in the museum has some uncial lettering on the cover.
examples.professional: The library catalogs its early Latin fragments by script, including several uncial manuscripts.
examples.analytical: Scholars date the codex by its uncial hand, which places it in the fourth or fifth century.

nuance.analogy: Like hand-painted capital letters on a medieval sign: round and separate, with no letters joined in a flowing line.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'uncialis' meaning an inch high or twelfth part, applied to the large letters of early manuscripts.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the c as a k or s sound instead of sh.
Confusing uncial with cursive, which is a joined, flowing handwriting style.

uncial.etymology: Attested 1650, from Latin *ū̆ncia* (“a twelfth part, ounce, inch”) + *-al*.

senses.definition: To take upon oneself; to start, to embark on.
senses.example: They undertook the new venture, not sure where it would lead.

senses.definition: To commit oneself (to an obligation, activity etc.).
senses.example: He undertook to exercise more in future.

core.definition: To take on a task, project or responsibility and begin working on it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAYK, the last syllable. The first syllable is weak, so say 'un-der' quickly. Make the final k sound crisp.

nuance.connotation: positive or neutral; it implies serious commitment to a demanding task.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use undertake in formal writing, proposals, and academic or business contexts, such as 'We will undertake a review.' In everyday speech people say 'take on,' 'start,' or 'do' instead. Undertake is less common in casual conversation but is natural in meetings and reports.

distinctions.note: Take on is informal and phrasal; undertake is more formal and suggests a serious commitment.
Begin is neutral and simple; undertake emphasizes a demanding or significant task.

examples.everyday: I'm going to undertake the kitchen remodel myself, though my husband thinks I'm crazy.
examples.professional: Our team will undertake a full audit of the pipeline before the next release.
examples.analytical: The theologian undertakes a close reading of Romans to test the claim that grace precedes faith.

nuance.analogy: Like rolling up your sleeves before a heavy job: you commit to doing the whole thing.
nuance.etymology: From under plus take, from Old English 'undertacan', to take in hand or undertake.
common_mistakes: Confusing undertake with 'undertaker', which means a funeral director in American English.
Using undertake with a preposition, such as 'undertake to something'; the verb takes a direct object.

senses.definition: Impossible to fathom.
senses.example: The sheer number of warriors the enemy attacked with was unfathomable.

senses.definition: Especially of depth: physically incapable of being measured; immeasurable.
Impossible to grasp the extent of, or to fully know or understand.
senses.example: The sheer number of warriors the enemy attacked with was unfathomable.

core.definition: Too deep, vast, or complex to be measured, understood, or fully grasped by the human mind.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FATH, and the th is voiced-unvoiced like the th in think. The -able ending reduces to uh-bul, so the word has four syllables, not five with an extra vowel after the m.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in descriptions of depth or size, but often strongly emotional when describing suffering, love, or mystery. It can sound like praise or like a complaint depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use unfathomable for things too large or deep to grasp: a loss, an act of cruelty, the size of the universe. It appears often in news, speeches, and personal conversation about grief or wonder. Saying something is unfathomable is a common way to express shock.

distinctions.note: Incomprehensible means impossible to understand at all; unfathomable suggests something whose depth or extent exceeds our grasp, though we may partly understand it.
Unimaginable means you cannot picture it; unfathomable stresses that it is too deep to fully understand, even if you can imagine parts of it.

examples.everyday: After the accident, my neighbor said the grief was unfathomable, and all we could do was bring her dinner.
examples.professional: The outage affected millions of users, and the scale of the impact was unfathomable until the dashboards finally loaded.
examples.analytical: Job's speeches describe God's ways as unfathomable, and the text invites the reader to accept that human reason cannot fully measure divine wisdom.

nuance.analogy: An unfathomable ocean is one whose bottom no sounding line can reach, no matter how long you let it down.
nuance.etymology: From un- plus fathomable, from fathom, from Old English faethm (outstretched arms, the span of the arms).
common_mistakes: Using unfathomable for things that are merely difficult; it implies depth or extent that exceeds full understanding.
Stressing the last syllable or adding an extra vowel after the m in the -able ending.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word anexereunētos (not searchable, unfathomable) appears in Romans 11:33, where Paul marvels at the unsearchable judgments and inscrutable ways of God. Job 11:7 asks whether a person can find out the deep things of God, which carries the same idea of human limits before divine depth. Both passages present God's ways as beyond full human comprehension.

senses.definition: Clumsy; lacking grace.
Gangling.
Difficult to move or to manage; unwieldy.
senses.example: The quotations in this entry are an ungainly assortment.

senses.definition: An ungainly person or thing.

core.definition: Awkward and clumsy in movement or shape; hard to manage or handle, lacking grace.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, GAYN, not on UN. The g is hard, as in 'go', and the final -ly is a clear 'lee'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes awkwardness, sometimes mildly unkind when used about people's bodies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ungainly for a person's walk or posture, a teenager going through a growth spurt, or a large object that is hard to carry. It can sound unkind if said directly about someone, so people often soften it with 'a bit ungainly' or use awkward instead. The word also appears in writing and speech about machines and furniture.

distinctions.note: Awkward is broader and covers social discomfort, while ungainly stresses physical clumsiness or bulk in movement or shape.
Gangly describes a thin, long-limbed body, while ungainly describes awkward movement or handling of anything, including objects.

examples.everyday: My little brother is at that ungainly stage where his legs seem too long for him.
examples.professional: The prototype is an ungainly design with too many cables, so the hardware team plans to simplify it before launch.
examples.analytical: Descriptions of the early church sometimes portray its structures as ungainly compared with later classical forms, yet this judgment reflects modern taste more than ancient purpose.

nuance.analogy: Like carrying a big cardboard box through a narrow door, where every step is clumsy.
nuance.etymology: From un- (not) plus gainly, from Middle English gayn, 'handy, convenient', so literally 'not handy'.
common_mistakes: Confusing ungainly with unprofitable or ungainful; the word is about awkward movement, not money.
Stressing the first syllable, as in UN-gainly; the stress falls on GAYN.

ungainly.etymology: From *un* + *gainly* (from *gain* (“dexterous; convenient, easy, handy; suitable”), from Old Norse *gegn* (“fit, serviceable; direct, straight; honest; kindly”) + *-ly*).

senses.definition: A fast-food combo of a main item, side and drink at a lower price than buying them separately.

core.definition: A fast-food bundle of a main item, a side, and a drink, sold for less than buying each item separately.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on VAL in this compound noun. Meal is pronounced like meel, and the two words run together lightly.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests a cheap, convenient deal, though it can imply low-cost fast food.
nuance.usage_note: At American fast-food restaurants, you might hear Can I get a value meal? or ask for a combo. Many chains now use combo meal or meal deal more often, so the term may vary by restaurant. A natural reply is to name your main item and drink, such as a cheeseburger value meal with a Coke.

distinctions.note: A combo meal means essentially the same thing, and many chains use it more often than value meal.
À la carte means ordering each item separately, usually at a higher total price.
A meal deal is a similar bundle, often used by sandwich shops or grocery stores.

examples.everyday: I'll just get the value meal with a Coke, since that's cheaper than buying everything separately.
examples.professional: Our value meal bundles drive most of the lunch-hour traffic, so the pricing needs review.
examples.analytical: The value meal is a pricing strategy that makes savings feel large, even when the cost per item is not much lower.

nuance.analogy: Like a prix fixe dinner at a diner: you pay one price for a set bundle instead of picking and paying for each part.
nuance.etymology: Value from Latin valere, to be worth; meal from Old English mæl, a measured portion of food or a time to eat.
common_mistakes: Using value meal for any inexpensive food; it specifically means a bundle of main, side, and drink.
Saying value menu when you mean the value meal; a value menu is a list of cheap items.

conversation.text: The value meal comes with a burger, fries and a drink.
I usually get the value meal because it's cheaper.
They raised the price of the value meal again.

senses.definition: The act of varying; a partial change in the form, position, state, or qualities of a thing.
A related but distinct thing.
senses.example: When the process didn't work, we tried a variation.

senses.definition: A line of play that differs from the original.
The modification of a hereditary trait.

The situation where two or more linguistic forms appear in the same environment without a change in meaning, the choice of form being determined by factors of dialect, sociolect, register or simply the speaker's preference.
An infinitesimal perturbation applied to a function, typically denoted δf, used to probe how a functional changes.
The corresponding first-order change in a functional induced by such a perturbation, typically denoted δJ[f] and called the first variation.
The angular difference at the vessel between the direction of true north and magnetic north.
A technique where material is repeated with alterations to the melody, harmony, rhythm, timbre, texture, counterpoint or orchestration; but with some invariant characteristic, e.g. a ground bass.
Deviation from the mean orbit of a heavenly body.

core.definition: A noticeable change or difference in something, such as form, amount, quality, or behavior, from what is typical or expected.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the syllable "ay," and the final syllable is a reduced "shun." The first vowel is the vowel in "bet," not the two-syllable "vair-ee" with a long e; say it smoothly as one flowing word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a difference without judging it as good or bad.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use variation in everyday and professional speech to mean a difference from the usual version, as in a variation on a recipe. People often say a variation of or a slight variation. In sports or music, it can name a different version of a play or piece. It sounds neutral in almost any situation, so it is a safe, polished choice.

distinctions.note: Variety refers to a range of different things in a set; variation refers to a change or version of a single thing.
Difference is a general word for how two things are not the same; variation implies a change from a standard or original.
A variant is a specific different form of something, often a noun used for a version of a word, gene, or product; variation is the general process or difference.

examples.everyday: This is a nice variation on my grandmother's chili recipe, with a little more cumin.
examples.professional: There's a lot of variation in how each team reports the same metric, so we need a standard definition.
examples.analytical: Human moral judgments show wide cultural variation, yet many philosophers argue that some core commitments persist across these differences.

nuance.analogy: Variation is like a song played in a new key: the melody is still recognizable, but something about it has shifted.
nuance.etymology: From Latin variatio, from variare, to change.
common_mistakes: Spelling or pronouncing it with an extra vowel, like "vair-ee-ay-shun" with too many syllables.
Using variation for a whole different thing rather than a change of something known.
Confusing it with variety, which describes a range of different items.

variation.etymology: From Middle French *variation*, from Old French *variacion*, from Latin *variātiō*, from *vary* + *-ation*.

senses.definition: Pertaining to or occurring in spring.
Having characteristics like spring; fresh, young, youthful.

core.definition: Relating to or happening in the spring; often used to suggest freshness and new growth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and keep the r rhotic. The final syllable is a reduced 'ul,' so it is not 'VER-nal' with a broad 'a.'

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests freshness, youth, and renewal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use vernal mostly in poetry, nature writing, and formal descriptions. In everyday talk, they say 'spring' or 'springtime.' The word appears in names like the 'vernal equinox,' which is the most common technical use.

distinctions.note: Spring is the everyday word for the season; vernal is a more formal or poetic adjective.
Springlike is a common, plain description of weather; vernal is more elevated and suggests renewal.

examples.everyday: The vernal weather this week makes everyone want to go outside.
examples.professional: We scheduled the planting for the vernal window, when soil temperatures are reliably above fifty degrees.
examples.analytical: The poem uses vernal imagery to suggest a new beginning after a long and painful winter of the soul.

nuance.analogy: Like the first warm morning after a cold winter, vernal describes a season that brings freshness and new life.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vernalis, from ver (spring).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the vowel as in 'ver' (rhyming with 'ever') instead of the American 'ur' sound.
Using vernal as an everyday word in place of 'spring' in ordinary conversation.

senses.definition: To treat (something) as inconsequential or worthless; to despise, to look down on.
To express a disparaging opinion of; to slander or vilify.

core.definition: To regard or speak of someone or something with contempt, as worthless.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second syllable short and quick. The final d is a clear 'd' sound. The word is rare in American speech, so the pronunciation is mainly for reading.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It expresses strong scorn or disdain for someone or something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use vilipend, and it is mostly found in older literature and formal writing. In everyday speech, people would say 'look down on,' 'disrespect,' or 'despise.' Use it only when you want a formal, literary tone.

distinctions.note: Despise is common and direct; vilipend is rare and literary, with a more formal, dignified tone.
Disparage means to speak of something as unimportant, often in a belittling way; vilipend adds a sense of treating it as worthless.

examples.everyday: My uncle said the new policy would make us look down on the people who cannot afford it, which I found hard to stomach.
examples.professional: The consultant warned that the committee must not vilipend the ideas of junior staff, even when they seem unrealistic.
examples.analytical: The essayist accused the critics of vilipending the peasantry while claiming to defend their interests.

nuance.analogy: To vilipend something is like treating a valuable antique as trash and tossing it aside.
nuance.etymology: From Latin vilipendere, 'to hold cheap,' from vilis, 'cheap,' and pendere, 'to weigh' or 'value.'
common_mistakes: Using vilipend in everyday conversation, where it sounds unnaturally formal.
Confusing it with vilify, which means to attack with harsh, damaging words.

vilipend.etymology: From Middle English *vilipenden* (“to treat as contemptible”), from Old French *vilipender*, or its etymon Latin *vilipendō*, from *vīlis* (“cheap, inexpensive; base, mean, vile, worthless”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European **wes-* (“to buy, sell”)) +…

senses.definition: A woman given to undue belligerence or ill manner at the slightest provocation.
A woman who is scolding, domineering, or highly opinionated.
A woman who is rough, loud, and aggressive.

core.definition: A woman who is loud, aggressive, domineering, or quick to argue, often in a negative way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'RAH', not the third. The 'a' is the open cot vowel, and the final 'o' is a long 'oh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative, implying a woman who is aggressive, scolding, or hard to handle. It can also be used with a note of admiration for a woman who is bold and strong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use virago in daily speech, and it is most common in literature, history, or witty commentary. Calling someone a virago in conversation can sound old-fashioned and insulting, so use it carefully. It is best understood when you recognize it in a novel or essay.

distinctions.note: Shrew is a stronger and more common insult for a bad-tempered woman. Virago is more literary and can suggest a bold, forceful woman as well.
Termagant is archaic and describes a quarrelsome, violent-tempered woman. Virago is closer to a loud, domineering woman.

examples.everyday: My grandmother called the loud neighbor a virago, but she was half joking.
examples.professional: Some reviewers described the lead character as a virago, which the author found unfair and sexist.
examples.analytical: The novel reconsiders the figure of the virago, turning a term of insult into a portrait of female authority.

nuance.analogy: A virago is like a storm inside a small room: loud, forceful, and hard to ignore.
nuance.etymology: From Latin virago, 'manly woman, heroine', from vir, 'man'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the last syllable, which makes the word sound wrong: 'vih-rah-GOH'.
Using it as a neutral word for any strong woman, when it usually carries a negative tone.

virago.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *virāgō* (“warlike or heroic woman”).

senses.definition: The act of visiting, or an instance of being visited.
An official visit to inspect or examine something.
An encounter with aliens or supernatural beings such as ghosts.
An affliction or disaster attributed to destiny, or to God.
The right of a separated or divorced parent to visit a child; access.
A punishment or blessing ordained by God.
An unusual and extensive irruption of a species of animals into another region.

core.definition: A formal or significant visit, especially an official inspection or a divine coming to help or judge people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -TAY-, and the 'si' in the middle is pronounced 'zih' before the stressed syllable. Be careful not to pronounce the middle 'i' as a long 'ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in official contexts; in religious contexts it may sound solemn or awe-inspiring.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use visitation most in official, religious or legal settings, such as a church pastoral visit or a court-ordered visit with a child. In ordinary conversation people say visit or stop by. Funeral homes in the US also use visitation for the period when mourners come to view the body.

distinctions.note: Visit is the everyday word for going to see someone, while visitation is more formal and often official or solemn.
Inspection stresses checking quality or compliance, while visitation may simply mean a formal call or a religious coming.

examples.everyday: My sister has visitation with her kids every other weekend, so she is free on Sundays.
examples.professional: The state auditors scheduled a visitation to review the clinic's records next month.
examples.analytical: In the Lukan narrative, the visitation of God is understood as a decisive intervention in history.

nuance.analogy: A visitation is like a visit with a formal invitation: it carries more weight and purpose than a casual drop-in.
nuance.etymology: From Latin visitatio, 'a visiting, a looking at,' from visitare, 'to visit often.'
common_mistakes: Using visitation for a casual visit to a friend, which sounds stiff.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'shin' instead of 'shun'.
nuance.biblical_note: The key Greek word is episkopē (ἐπισκοπή), meaning a looking upon, inspection or divine visit. In Scripture it often signals God coming to examine, save or judge his people. Luke 1:68 speaks of God having visited and redeemed his people, presenting the visitation as an act of saving grace. Luke 19:44 warns Jerusalem that it did not recognize the time of its visitation, meaning the moment of God's coming. 1 Peter 2:12 urges believers to glorify God on the day of visitation, presenting that day as the time of his decisive coming.

visitation.etymology: From Anglo-Norman *visitacioun*, from Old French *visitacion*, from Latin *vīsitātiō*.

senses.definition: Something in the past that cannot be controlled or undone, but must be accepted, forgiven, or forgotten.
senses.example: They agreed that their old disputes were water under the bridge and decided to make a fresh start.

core.definition: Something that happened in the past that is no longer important and should be forgiven or forgotten.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on BRIDGE, and the phrase is said quickly, so under and the are reduced. The t in water is a soft American flap that sounds like a d.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive: it signals letting go, often used to end an argument kindly, though it can sound dismissive if the hurt is serious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this casually when an old quarrel or small mistake is over, for example after a friend apologizes. A natural reply is Yeah, it's water under the bridge, or Don't worry about it. Avoid it for serious harm or ongoing injustice, where it sounds dismissive.

distinctions.note: Bygones be bygones is more formal and somewhat old-fashioned; water under the bridge is the everyday American version.
Forgive and forget describes a deliberate moral choice; water under the bridge is more casual and focuses on the past no longer mattering.

collocations: that's all water under the bridge
let it be water under the bridge
forget it, it's water under the bridge

examples.everyday: You forgot my birthday last year? That's water under the bridge, so let's grab lunch.
examples.professional: The missed deadline on the old project is water under the bridge; let's focus on the new timeline.
examples.analytical: Some argue that past injustices are water under the bridge, but moral responsibility does not simply expire with time.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that has already flowed past the bridge: you cannot stop it, and you cannot use that same water again.
nuance.etymology: Idiom from the image of a river flowing past a bridge; exact origin unknown.
common_mistakes: Using it literally about real water; it is always figurative.
Using it for a serious crime or harm, where it sounds callous.

conversation.text: We had a fight years ago, but it's water under the bridge now.
"Sorry about last week." "Don't worry. It's water under the bridge."
That old disagreement with the vendor is water under the bridge.

senses.definition: Introduces your summary of what someone said, to check you understood.

core.definition: A professional phrase used to introduce your summary of what someone said, so you can check that you understood correctly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on HEAR-, the main syllable of hearing. The phrase flows as one unit: wuh-tahym-HEER-ing-iz, with I'm sounding like ahym and is reduced to iz.

nuance.connotation: Positive and professional; it shows active listening and helps prevent misunderstandings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in meetings, coaching sessions, and conflict conversations to reflect back what they heard. It sounds natural when followed by a short summary and a question, such as 'Is that right?' Avoid using it as a sarcastic way to disagree.

distinctions.note: More casual and can sound skeptical or confrontational; what I'm hearing is is softer and more collaborative.
Signals a conclusion; what I'm hearing is invites correction and checks understanding.

collocations: Let me make sure I understand: what I'm hearing is
